# Task: High-Performance Three.js Tactical Map Engine & Canvas Module Build a production-quality, high-performance **Three.js Tactical Terrain & Map Engine** (`terrainEngine.ts` + `harness.html`). It renders a rugged mountain canyon, road network, residential neighborhood, and dynamic emergency overlays (glowing routes, fire perimeters, tactical unit chips, and a drone camera HUD). Modeled on professional wildfire emergency command displays (FireTrace / CAL FIRE tactical systems). The deliverable is a **headless TypeScript module with an exposed API + a standalone runnable test harness**, designed to be controlled by an external UI shell. --- ## 1. Visual Direction: "GLOW-AS-STATE" This is a **night tactical command instrument** (03:00 AM low-visibility wildland fire ops), NOT a colorful game diorama. - **Matte Hypsometric Terrain**: Dark slate-black (`#0A0E14` to `#1C2530`) with high-contrast shaded relief. - **Topographic Contour Isolines**: Clean 20m elevation contour lines injected into the terrain shader (antialiased, view-independent). - **Glow-as-State**: The physical world is dark and matte. ONLY active operational state emits light: * Active Evacuation Route: Luminous Cyan (`#00E5FF`) with animated forward chevrons. * Standby Route: Dashed Amber warning ribbon (`#FF8A4A`). * Compromised Choke Point: Solid Red (`#E5533C`) with hazard marker. * Active Flame Front: Emissive Fire Orange (`#FF6A00`) with glowing boundary and thermal hotspots. - **Zero Toy 3D Vehicles**: Units are rendered as clean tactical chips or point markers, never 3D toy meshes. --- ## 2. Landscape & Geographical Elements Required The scene represents a high-risk Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) coastal canyon (6000m E-W × 3250m N-S): 1. **Mountain Crests & Canyons**: Ridge peaks (~490m) dropping into steep chaparral canyons and coastal valleys. 2. **Road Network**: - Primary coastal highway along the southern edge. - Winding two-lane canyon arterial climbing the ridge. - Residential cul-de-sacs and neighborhood access streets. 3. **Residential Neighborhood**: Building footprints (canyon homes, ranches, cottages) clustered along access roads in the valley and ridge benches. 4. **Vegetation Zones**: Differentiated land-cover shading (dense chaparral/timber slopes vs. bare rock ridge tops). --- ## 3. Data Interface — Dual Source (Real + Procedural Fallback) The engine supports both real data and an autonomous procedural fallback: - **Procedural Fixture (Default)**: If no external files are loaded, generate the complete terrain elevation (Simplex/Perlin multi-octave ridges), procedural winding road graph, and residential building clusters inline so `harness.html` runs immediately with zero attachments. - **Real Data Loaders**: Clean async `loadWorldData(basePath)` fetching: * `dem.bin` (Int16 LE, 400 cols × 220 rows, 15m cells, elevations in metres −1 to 491m). * `frame.json` (`{"center": {"lat": 34.032, "lon": -118.815}, "widthMeters": 6000.0, "heightMeters": 3250.0}`). * `roads.json` (`[{id, kind, width, points: [[x, y], ...]}]`). * `buildings.json` (`[{id, kind, height, footprint: [[x, y], ...]}]`). ### Coordinate Law (Exact) Local metres, origin at frame center: **+x east, +y north**. Frame 6000 × 3250 m. worldX = (col / (cols - 1)) * 6000 - 3000 worldY = 1625 - (row / (rows - 1)) * 3250 Three.js is Y-up: World `(x, elev, y)` maps to scene `(x, elev, -y)`. **Critical**: Sample elevation with **bilinear interpolation** so draped road ribbons and building bases stay perfectly anchored to the ground without clipping or floating. --- ## 4. Two Cameras, One Mesh (Instant Toggle) - **A. Top-Down Orthographic (2D Topo)**: Straight nadir, camera up = North. Legible, calm map with 20m contour isolines and lat/long edge ticks (34.03°N, 118.81°W). - **B. Perspective Tactical View (3D)**: Smooth animated camera tween to 55° pitch / -30° bearing showing mountain relief, canyon depths, and draped ribbons. *Switching cameras is a pure camera projection/position tween—never a re-creation of geometry.* --- ## 5. Overlays, Tactical Chips & In-Canvas Drone PiP 1. **Dynamic Overlays API**: - `engine.setOverlayLayer(id, spec)` supporting polygons (including darkened burn-scar interior masks) and screen-space fat lines (`Line2`) draped 3m over terrain via bilinear elevation sampling. - Includes Route A (cyan `#00E5FF` with animated forward chevrons), Route B (dashed amber `#FF8A4A`), Compromised Choke Point (solid red `#E5533C`), and Active Fire Perimeter (emissive orange `#FF6A00`). 2. **Tactical Resource Chips (DOM / CSS2D — Zero Emojis)**: - Render crisp, high-contrast dark tactical pills (`#0A0E14` background, 1px subtle border, monospace telemetry, inline geometric SVG icons or glowing status dots—NEVER use OS color emojis): * Ground units clamped to terrain surface: `[ ▲ E-31 · Type 3 ]`, `[ ■ C-7 · Hotshots ]` * Airborne drones hovering at 3D AGL altitude with a subtle 3D loiter orbit path and a semi-transparent vertical altitude drop-line (stalk) to the ground below: `[ ● FT-01 · 1,930 ft ]`, `[ ● FT-06 · 740 ft ]` 3. **In-Canvas Drone Gimbal PiP Window**: - Clicking `FT-06` (or calling `engine.openDronePip("FT-06")`) opens a draggable floating HUD window inside the viewport. - Render a live secondary `PerspectiveCamera` view from `FT-06`'s 3D position and gimbal angle (Pitch `-27°`, Heading `112°`) looking down at the active flame front (using `setScissor`/`setViewport` or a PiP canvas). - Include a live toggle inside the PiP between `[EO Night]` and `[IR Thermal (Ironbow false-color)]`, a military reticle overlay, telemetry readout (`ALT 740 FT AGL · HDG 112° · PITCH -27°`), and a locked thermal hotspot marker (`980°C` core temp + lat/lon coordinates). --- ## 6. Strict Recruiter Performance Budget A portfolio recruiter must be able to open this on a laptop with zero lag: - **≤ 20 draw calls** at rest (batch buildings into a single InstancedMesh; merge road geometries). - **≤ 200k triangles**. - **0% GPU draw when static**: Dirty-flagged on-demand rendering (no unconditional requestAnimationFrame loop). - Device pixel ratio capped at 1.25×. - No dynamic shadow maps (use baked normal/hypsometric shading). --- ## 7. Deliverables 1. **`terrainEngine.ts`**: Clean, modular TypeScript Three.js engine exporting: - `createTerrainEngine(container, options)` → `Engine` - `engine.setCamera("topdown" | "perspective", durationMs)` - `engine.setThermal(boolean)` - `engine.setVerticalExaggeration(scale, durationMs)` (e.g., `1.0x` in 2D, `2.0x` in 3D) - `engine.setOverlayLayer(id, spec)` - `engine.openDronePip(droneId)` / `engine.closeDronePip()` - `engine.flyTo({ position, target, durationMs })` - `engine.getMetrics()` → `{ drawCalls, triangles, fps }` - `engine.dispose()` 2. **`harness.html`**: A self-contained, zero-build-step runnable test harness (using `<script type="importmap">` loading `three` and `three/addons/` from CDN so it runs immediately in any browser without a bundler). Includes: - Top-down 2D Topo, 3D Perspective, Vertical Exaggeration (`1x | 2x`), and Thermal toggles. - Live `Draw Calls / Triangles / FPS` telemetry counter. - Layer toggle buttons, camera `flyTo` presets, and clickable `FT-06` chip opening the live Gimbal PiP HUD. - ## 8. Priority Order 1. Terrain mesh + procedural canyon + 2D Topo / 3D Perspective camera tween. 2. Road network + residential building footprints (instanced, clamped to terrain). 3. The overlay API with 1 active evacuation route (cyan chevrons) + 1 fire perimeter. 4. Tactical unit chips + floating in-canvas Drone Gimbal PiP HUD. 5. Thermal (IR) grading pass.

# 👋 MiMo Arena — start here

This workspace puts Xiaomi's **MiMo-V2.6-Pro** and **MiMo-V2.6-Flash** (released 2026-09-21) into the
Models Arena: the same blind, Arena-style tests DS-Arena ran on DeepSeek, against the same opponents —
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon and Kimi K3. Claude judges and never competes.
Everything in this workspace is in English.

## 1 · Watch the evaluation: the pinned sessions

| | session | what to look at |
|---|---|---|
| ① | **MiMo Arena ① SVG: pelican on a bicycle** | Simon Willison's pelican plus two unseen prompts; per-image scores |
| ② | **MiMo Arena ② WebDev one-shot** | screenshot battles of three single-file pages; Xiaomi's front-end claim |
| ③ | **MiMo Arena ③ Deterministic traps** | hidden tests, a 150k-token log, phantom-entity probes |
| ④ | **MiMo Arena ④ Agent tool use** | mock-tool trajectories: retries, symlinks, prompt injection, impossible meetings |
| ⑤ | **MiMo Arena ⑤ Translation & writing** | zh/en/ja translation, a 100-word horror story, Chinese essay, role-play |
| ⑥ | **MiMo Arena ⑥ English community cases** | what English-speaking testers tried on MiMo-V2.6, reproduced blind |

Every session follows the same order: run the models → build anonymous battles → fresh-context judge
subagents → reveal → audit → report.

## 2 · Results and data

| want | open |
|---|---|
| Final report | `arena/results/official/FINAL_REPORT.md` |
| Scenario reports | `arena/results/official/s1_svg/REPORT.md` … `s6_english/REPORT.md` |
| Pooled tables | `arena/results/official/aggregate.md` |
| English-community cases and claims | `mimo_eval_cases.md` |
| Judge protocol / iteration log | `arena/JUDGING.md` · `arena/ITERATIONS.md` |
| Raw replies, renders, battle packets, verdicts | `arena/runs/official/` |

## 3 · Try it yourself

Open a new session here and ask, e.g. "show me MiMo-V2.6-Pro's pelicans next to GPT's" or
"which S4 runs did MiMo-V2.6-Flash fail, and why?". To re-run or add a scenario see `arena/README.md`.

This workspace evaluates Xiaomi **MiMo-V2.6-Pro** and **MiMo-V2.6-Flash** Arena-style against the DS-Arena roster
(DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, Kimi K3). Claude is the blind judge, never a contestant.
Work and write in **English**.

- `/data/ws/deepseek` is the sibling DS-Arena workspace and the public showcase source. Read it if useful; do not modify it from here.

# NIGHTDRIVE // ISO–86 — Anatomy edition

Open `index.html` directly in a browser. The app is a single self-contained file with no external runtime dependencies.

The latest pass rebuilds all three cars using the [Anatomy](https://skills.wheresryan.sh/anatomy) modeling workflow. Each vehicle has more than 200 modeled components, including actual wheel openings, rounded tires, separate rims and brakes, cockpit parts, chassis and powertrain assemblies. The Spinner floats above the road with four downward thrusters and illuminated ground footprints.

**Space / Cutaway** pauses the drive and opens the vehicle inspection stage. Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, and use **Assembled**, **Exploded**, or the separation slider. **Return to drive** restores the original camera and paused/running state. The garage cards switch the inspected vehicle.

The live scene now uses dependency-free WebGL with a depth buffer and retained mesh buffers. This resolves overlapping wheel/body surfaces and inconsistent occlusion between the two city corridors. Real 3D meshes remain in use throughout; no building images are baked. SVG remains a reduced-detail fallback, using the original preallocated pools.

The city has aligned primary setbacks on both sides, taller secondary rows, six additional cyberpunk frontage types, sky-pipes and delivery drones. Streetlamps have visible emitters and projected pools. Headlights cast brighter road illumination. The existing synth and microphone input remain available.

Travel is calibrated at eight world units per meter and advances by real elapsed time, making the indicated speed about five times faster than the preceding build at the same slider value. This removes frame-count dependence from travel. It does not establish a sustained 60 FPS result on hardware: the available test browser uses software graphics, so hardware frame-rate verification remains outstanding.

Validation for this edition:

```sh
node nightdrive-iso86/qa/anatomy/audit.mjs
node nightdrive-iso86/qa/anatomy/verify.mjs
```

- 26/26 functional checks passed, including inspection pause/resume, hover and thrusters, lighting, audio, mobile fit and frame-independent travel.
- 217,360 sampled body-surface points across the two road cars produced no tire-clearance violations.
- The SVG fallback stayed within its 2,400-slot capacity (2,380 peak), with no runtime errors.
- This is a custom mesh audit of the actual application geometry, not a claim that Anatomy’s native turning-kit audit was run.

The downloaded skill and license are preserved in `.reference-skills/anatomy/`; the design treatment, screenshots and test reports are in `qa/anatomy/`. Earlier implementation notes follow for historical context and describe the superseded renderer.

# NIGHTDRIVE // ISO–86

A full-screen, interactive night drive through a procedural isometric city. Open `index.html` in a browser. No install, server, network connection, build step, downloaded models, or external runtime libraries are needed.

The updated scene uses opaque, shaded geometry throughout: a silver AE–86, Countach and Kusanagi silhouettes, a twenty-slot roadside conveyor, ten reusable architectural models, an elevated three-lane expressway, viaduct supports, utility conduits, a metro train, streetlamps, sign gantries and three-rib overpass portals. The camera can move between an isometric view and a rear chase view.

## Controls

| Action | Control |
| --- | --- |
| Steer | Move the mouse across the scene, or A / D / left / right |
| Orbit | Drag the scene |
| Zoom | Mouse wheel |
| Mechanical cutaway | Space or **Cutaway** |
| Switch car | 1 / 2 / 3 or garage cards |
| Headlights | L or sun button |
| Camera preset | C or **Isometric / Chase** |
| City / mountains / hybrid | W or mountain button |
| Pause / resume | P or pause button |
| Cinema view | H or cinema button; Escape exits |

ThinkingI'll settle on keeping terrainEngine.ts as the source and compiling it to a readable terrainEngine.js module. The harness will try importing it normally when served over http, and fall back to an inlined blob version for file:// access, with a build script keeping both in sync. I should also decide whether to generate sample data files like dem.bin, frame.json, roads.json, and buildings.json to match the real data loaders the spec calls for.
I'm checking that puppeteer-core and three are available locally, since the harness relies on CDN imports. Since browsers can't execute .ts files directly, I need a zero-build approach: either ship a pre-compiled terrainEngine.js alongside the .ts source, or have the harness transpile TypeScript in-browser using something like esbuild-wasm or sucrase. But I realize ES module imports over file:// trigger CORS failures in Chrome, so a harness.html that imports a local .js file won't just work when double-clicked — people need to serve it via a local server. To make it truly self-contained, I'm considering inlining the compiled engine directly into harness.html via a build step, since CDN-hosted modules do work over file:// thanks to permissive CORS headers, unlike local file imports. I'll settle on keeping terrainEngine.ts as the source and compiling it to a readable terrainEngine.js module. The harness will try importing it normally when served over http, and fall back to an inlined blob version for file:// access, with a build script keeping both in sync. I should also decide whether to generate sample data files like dem.bin, frame.json, roads.json, and buildings.json to match the real data loaders the spec calls for.

ThinkingFound it: vDist is computed per-vertex and interpolated linearly across a massive 48km quad, so the fragment shader gets an averaged distance (~25km) instead of the true per-pixel distance to camera. That inflates the fog factor to near 1 everywhere. The fix is to compute distance in the fragment shader using the actual world position relative to camera instead of relying on the interpolated vertex value.
Comparing the pixel colors, I notice the pale tone matches the fog color almost exactly, suggesting the ocean shader is outputting near-total fog factor rather than actual water color — likely a fresnel or density issue with the fog uniform passed into the ocean material. Fog density at that distance gives too little contribution to explain the paleness, so that's not it. The output color is almost exactly equal to uFogColor itself — meaning the fresnel mix must be pushing all the way toward fog color rather than the ocean's deep blue, which is the real explanation for why it looks so pale. Found it: vDist is computed per-vertex and interpolated linearly across a massive 48km quad, so the fragment shader gets an averaged distance (~25km) instead of the true per-pixel distance to camera. That inflates the fog factor to near 1 everywhere. The fix is to compute distance in the fragment shader using the actual world position relative to camera instead of relying on the interpolated vertex value.

The ocean shades as pure fog because vDist is interpolated across a 48 km quad, so even pixels near the camera get about 25 km. Computing the distance per fragment instead:

For routing, I plan to filter down to just the Encinal Canyon Road and PCH segments and build a dedicated RoadNetwork from only those roads, avoiding the complexity of per-road cost penalties since the cost function only sees midpoint coordinates. Route A connects the northernmost Encinal point to the PCH's westmost junction, while Route B continues east along PCH-only roads from that junction to the eastern edge; I also need to compute the hairpin turn by scanning 150m windows along the Encinal polyline and isolating the choke-point arc around the tightest turn. Finally I'm setting up building cluster detection using union-find with a 130m linkage threshold over centroids. Draw calls (target ≤ 20)

  • 13 at rest, 19 with the drone feed open (it was 23 before I trimmed the feed pass).

Decisions for you

  • Triangle budget. At your requested counts, the trees and shrubs alone add 204k triangles. The main view is about 405k on the procedural map and 418k on Encinal. Without vegetation it's 201k and 214k; Encinal is higher because of its 1,106 real buildings. Counts are adjustable with the vegetation: { trees, shrubs } option. To get back under 200k I can either cut counts to roughly 2.5k trees and 3.5k shrubs, or lower the terrain mesh resolution. The harness shows the vegetation share separately so it's visible either way.
  • Encinal isn't in your original frame. The spec's center (34.032°N, 118.815°W) covers Zuma and Point Dume; Encinal Canyon Road lies entirely west and north of it. The real-data frame.json uses 34.0465°N, 118.872°W, same 6 × 3.25 km size and 400 × 220 grid. That frame contains the ocean, PCH, the lower Encinal switchbacks and Trancas Canyon.

1. 3D vegetation

  • One instanced mesh of 6,000 trees (14 triangles each) and one of 10,000 shrubs (12 each).
  • Each sits on the terrain via bilinear DEM sampling; tree heights scale with vertical exaggeration.
  • Trees inside the burn scar collapse to charred, glowing snags.
  • loadWorldData() reads vegetation.json (ESA WorldCover classes: 10 → trees, 20 → shrubs). Without it, placement falls back to slope and elevation.

2. Day/Night

  • New engine.setLighting('day' | 'night', ms), which tweens a shared uDayNight uniform (0 = night, 1 = day).
  • Day mode uses your palette, with sun from the southeast at 10:30, white road edges and off-white buildings.
  • The drone feed switches between EO Day and EO Night. Thermal by day shows sun-warmed slopes.
  • The toggle uses drawn sun and moon icons instead of ☀️/🌙, to keep the spec's no-OS-emoji rule.

3. Extended environment

  • An ocean plane runs out about 24 km, with surf along the real shoreline, sun glint by day and moon glint at night.
  • A procedural mountain ring surrounds the frame, joined to its edge with no visible seam. On real data this terrain is invented.
  • THREE.FogExp2 haze matches a gradient sky drawn behind the canvas, which costs no draw call.

4. Encinal Canyon scenario

  • npm run data downloads real terrain (AWS Terrain Tiles), OpenStreetMap roads and buildings, and ESA WorldCover land cover into data/.
  • It then builds scenario.json:
    • A fictional fire runs across the ridge from Trancas Canyon.
    • Zones 1–3 are drawn from clusters of real buildings.
    • The cyan route follows the real Encinal Canyon Road down to PCH, then west.
    • The choke marker sits on the real 80° hairpin.
    • Units E-31, E-32, a Sheriff unit and drone FT-01 are placed on real roads.
  • The harness labels it a training scenario and shows the data attributions.

{ hud: false } already existed; it's now documented and tested.

Frame rates in my tests come from a software renderer, so they don't predict laptop performance.

# Product Requirement: Multi-Phase Operational Flow Map & Timeline Scrubber The physical engine substrate (Day/Night, 3D instanced vegetation, 24km ocean, Encinal Canyon frame) is verified and running within budget (13 draw calls, 0.6ms CPU). Now we must fulfill the core architectural requirement: **Sentinel is an emergency command platform, NOT a single-scene wildfire demo.** The map engine must be a general-purpose GIS substrate capable of showing Routine Standby (Peace-Time), and transitioning dynamically through a complete 5-stage incident lifecycle. To keep the codebase maintainable, follow a clean 3-tier architecture: - `terrainEngine.ts`: Pure, incident-agnostic WebGL engine. It renders terrain, foliage, infrastructure, and generic layer primitives (`setOverlayLayer`, `setUnits`). - `data/scenario.json`: Declarative flow map defining the 5 phases, coordinates, isochrones, routes, and unit positions. - `harness.html`: Testbed UI with an interactive incident timeline scrubber. --- ### The 5 Operational Phases to Implement in `scenario.json`: 1. **Phase 0: Routine Watch (Peace-Time Baseline)** - Default state upon launch. Clean topography, calm day or night, clean roads, zero fires, zero evacuation zones. - 1 Drone (`FT-01 Kite`) flying a routine surveillance waypoint sweep across the canyon. - Normal weather telemetry (12 mph SW, RH 38%, 68°F). 2. **Phase 1: Intel & Anomaly Detection** - Hotspot detected at Trancas Ridge (`34.048° N, 118.868° W`). - Pulsing amber anomaly beacon appears on map. - `FT-01` breaks routine orbit and flies to the target. Gimbal PiP opens in thermal mode verifying smoke/ignition. 3. **Phase 2: TALON Modeling & Escalation** - Active flame front appears (`#FF6A00` glow + embers) with developing burn scar. - TALON spread isochrones appear: +15 min (solid), +30 min (dashed amber), +60 min (critical red). - Residential buildings within the 60-min isochrone are highlighted (`threatened`). 4. **Phase 3: Evacuation & Route Design (Plan Formulation)** - Evacuation Zones 1 (Mandatory red hatch), 2 (Warning amber), and 3 (Safe PCH staging). - Primary Route A (Encinal Canyon Rd to PCH) in glowing cyan (`#00E5FF`) with flow chevrons. - Alternate Route B (Lachman Lane ridge detour) in dashed amber (`#FF8A4A`). - Choke point warning marker at the 80° switchback hairpin. - Interactive Route Swap: Clicking Route B promotes it to active cyan and turns Route A amber. Provide API: `engine.setActiveRoute('route-a' | 'route-b')`. 5. **Phase 4: Field Operations & Mutual Aid Coordination (Execution)** - Mutual-aid units appear on the roads: Engines E-31 & E-32, Bulldozer DZ-3 on fire flank, Sheriff SH-12 holding the hairpin choke point. - Live breadcrumbs advance along the road network. --- ### UI & Engine Integration: - In `terrainEngine.ts`: Expose `engine.setPhase(index: 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4, durationMs?: number)` which smoothly transitions layers and camera. - In `harness.html`: Add an interactive **Incident Timeline Scrubber Bar** across the bottom: `[ ◀ Prev ] [ Phase 0: Standby | Phase 1: Detect | Phase 2: Model | Phase 3: Plan | Phase 4: Execute ] [ Next ▶ ] [ ▶ Auto-Play ]` - Maintain strict performance (≤ 20 draw calls, 0% GPU draw when parked). read the two documents as well and tell me do they makes sense properly for the whole product concept?

Mostly yes. Both documents describe the same product: a situational map for an incident's whole lifecycle, driven by scenario data, starting from a calm standby state. 12-incident-flow is the stronger of the two and should be the contract. The charter and your PRD contradict it in several places and contain some factual errors about the site. I checked those claims against the real data in data/. I haven't started building, because some of these would get baked into the code.

Where the two documents conflict

  1. Two documents both say they are canonical, with different phase models. Doc 12 has seven phases (A–G); the charter has five (0–4).

    • A→0, B→1, C→2, D→3 and F→4 line up.
    • E (Authorized) is missing from the charter. It is folded into the 3→4 transition.
    • G (Revision) is reduced to a route-swap button.

    Those two are the phases doc 12 calls most important.

  2. Where phase logic lives. Doc 12 §5 says "the engine knows nothing about fire, plans, or incidents." Your PRD says the same, then puts setPhase() and setActiveRoute('route-a' | 'route-b') on the engine. A route ID baked into the engine API is incident logic. Phases should sit in a separate scenario player that reads scenario.json and calls the generic engine API.

  3. The route swap breaks doc 12's main rule. In the charter, clicking Route B immediately makes it cyan. Doc 12 says a revision is a ghosted draft shown next to the committed plan, and the operator approves it.

  4. Proposed and committed plans look the same. In the charter, Phase 3 routes already glow cyan before anything is authorized, so the plan looks committed before it is.

  5. Dashed amber means four different things. In the charter it is Route B, the +30 min isochrone and Zone 2. Doc 12 also uses amber, ghosted and thin for a draft. The documents need one styling scale: proposed / committed / draft / compromised.

  6. Automatic actions vs operator control. In the charter the drone retasks itself and the PiP opens on its own. Doc 12 says the operator dispatches the drone, and "TALON never moves furniture."

  7. Scope. Doc 12 requires three situation files: standby, small incident and WUI breakout. The small incident is the test that proves the map isn't fire-only. The PRD has one file and omits the small incident.

Problems inside the charter / PRD

  1. The timeline undermines the plan.

    • Isochrones are computed at 00:45, and the +60 line crosses Encinal Canyon Rd at about 01:45.
    • The Phase 3 plan (01:30) sends evacuees down that road, and authorization happens in Phase 4 at 02:30.
    • So people are routed through a road the model says burned 45 minutes earlier.
    • Possible fix: let the fire compromise Route A during Operations. TALON then drafts Route B and the operator approves it. That turns doc 12's Phase G into the route swap.

  2. The wind contradicts the fire. Wind from the WSW pushes the fire east-northeast, inland and away from Encinal and PCH. A run from the Trancas side toward Encinal and the coast needs a NE/E (Santa Ana) wind. RH of 18% also goes with a Santa Ana, not an onshore breeze. The Phase 0 weather also differs between the documents (12 mph SW / RH 38% vs 8 mph WSW / RH 42%).

  3. Site facts, checked against data/:

    • Lachman Lane is in Pacific Palisades, about 20 km east, and isn't in the frame. Real alternates in the frame are PCH east (the current Route B) or Decker Road.
    • The hotspot (34.048°N, 118.868°W) sits 1.7 km west of Trancas Canyon Rd and 0.5 km from Encinal, so it isn't "Trancas Ridge." The schema's [625, 980] is a different point, and the current build ignites at a third point, (2150, 1300) in Trancas Canyon. Pick one.
    • "1,106 residential buildings" is every OSM building in the frame, not just homes.
    • "47 threatened" and "14 ft clearance" are typed in as facts. Doc 12 rule 2 says to compute them or label them as authored. The 47 should come from the isochrone. The 14 ft has no source.
    • "⚠️" breaks the no-emoji rule.

  4. Domain wording:

    • Rothermel's model is 1972, not 1974.
    • ICS-209 is a status report form, not a phase framework.
    • MODIS/VIIRS satellites can't realistically flag a 2.4-acre fire within minutes. For Malibu, a 911 call or a fire-watch camera network such as ALERTCalifornia is the believable trigger.
    • An "unverified" detection shouldn't carry an acreage (doc 12: a detection is a point).
    • A dNBR burn scar (doc 12's catalogue) is a post-fire satellite product, so it can't exist in the first hour.

  5. The schema isn't scrubbable as written.

    • Each phase lists only what changes, without geometry, so it's unclear what carries forward. Doc 12 rule 7 requires scrubbing back to restore the earlier state exactly.
    • Better: each layer gets a validity window (from/until), and the map state at time t is computed purely from those windows.
    • The timeline runs to 04:00, but the last phase is at 02:30.

  6. The draw-call budget breaks with the feed open.

    • Adding the isochrones, beacon, breadcrumbs, dozer line and triage takes the main view to about 18–19. Opening the drone feed (+6) goes over 20.
    • Fix: draw isochrones as contours of the fire's arrival-time field inside the terrain shader. That costs 0 draw calls, matches the perimeter exactly and scrubs with one number.
    • Batch all route lines into one mesh.

  7. Night-style rule vs daylight standby. Doc 12 rule 5 says the terrain is dark and only operational data glows. That doesn't fit a daylight standby with a blue ocean. Decide whether the day palette is muted or the rule applies only at night.

Proposed approach

  • Engine: stays generic. It gains time-windowed layers with crossfades and a style-state field (proposed / committed / draft / compromised).
  • New scenarioPlayer.ts: owns setPhase and route promotion, the latter as draft → approve.
  • Scenario files: three, following doc 12, generated from real roads by the existing tools script.
  • Scrubber: seven stops, or five with Authorize as a button inside Plan and Revision as an event inside Execute.
  • Fire: NE wind; the ignition point is your call (item 10).
  • Route B: PCH east.

If you're happy with these defaults I'll build on them. Otherwise tell me which of items 1, 8, 9 and 10 to settle differently.

For moving units along roads, rather than rebuilding instance buffers every frame via repeated setUnits calls, I'm leaning toward giving the engine a generic time concept: units carry a track with a path and timestamps, and the engine evaluates positions via a single setTime(t) call that also drives other time-aware layers like isochrones and trails. This keeps the engine free of fire-specific knowledge while making scrubbing cheap, with the player just setting layers once per phase and driving time externally. Scoping the actual work now: the engine needs a tweened setSceneTime/getSceneTime method, plus a new time-field overlay type that renders burned area, an active front glow, and isochrone contours at fixed time offsets from an arrival-time texture, added alongside (not replacing) the existing polygon-based fire modes to avoid breaking the procedural demo. I'm also considering adding a state property to line styling for proposed versus other states. I'm tallying up the draw-call budget — currently around 13 for terrain, ocean, roads, buildings, trees, shrubs, routes, fire front, hotspots, units, and drone stalks — and checking how much headroom Phase 4 additions like breadcrumbs, dozer lines, draft routes, and anomaly beacons would eat into, trying to keep separate line and marker layers from pushing the count too high. Batching all the line overlays into a single Line2 mesh would require moving per-layer style properties like color, dash, and glow into per-vertex attributes, which means a significant shader refactor, so I'm weighing whether that's worth it versus just excluding annotations from the sensor feed pass since physical layers like roads are fine there. Before deciding, I want to check whether marker layers are already consolidated into one mesh. For the scenario player, I'm considering putting it in its own module that only imports types from the terrain engine and receives an engine instance, then checking how build.mjs inlines files to make sure it can inline this too for the file:// loading case. I also need to look at the three scenario JSON files and the generator script that produces them. To keep backward compatibility, I'll make the player treat a flat scenario without `phases` as a single-phase situation, so scenario.json keeps working as-is while the new phased flow files are additive. For the procedural harness, the timeline scrubber raises a question: should it also work with procedural-generated worlds, or should the timeline just be a real-data feature with procedural staying single-phase? If I want shared phase composition, it'd need a generic function that builds an incident arc from any world, which could live alongside the existing demo scenario builder rather than duplicating logic. For the actual harness layout, I'm sketching out the controls: a time scrubber with phase tick marks, prev/next and auto-play buttons, a clock readout, a situation selector (Standby/Small incident/WUI breakout), plan approval buttons, and provenance labels in the layer list. I should avoid the "◀ ▶" text glyphs since those Unicode arrows can sometimes render as emoji on certain platforms — better to use inline SVG arrows for consistency. For verify.mjs, I'm planning checks that each phase applies cleanly, draw calls stay under budget, scrubbing back restores exact prior state, scenario switching doesn't throw console errors, and standby mode shows no fire layers. I also need to confirm small incidents have no perimeter rendering, phases D and E share identical geometry via a hash comparison, and static parked states show zero animated frames. Time to stop planning and dig into the actual code structure.

async function loadEngine() {
  try {

    const src = document.getElementById('tte-engine-inline').textContent;
    if (!src || src.length < 1000) throw err;

    return await import(url);
  }
}

ThinkingBefore touching the README, I should decide on the actual route geometry—working through where the scaled fire crosses encinalMain, which buildings sit north of that crossing, and where the frame edge falls—so I can proceed efficiently through builder, engine, player, and harness in order.
I'm sketching the architecture now, planning a scene clock in the terrain engine that drives a uniform time value for overlays and unit tracking, aiming for something solid but scoped. For the arrival-time field overlay I'm working out a spec that holds a per-cell grid of arrival times usable generically for fire, flood, or plume simulations, with options for a burn-scar fill, an active front band, and labeled isochrone contours. On the rendering side, I'm figuring out how to feed this as a float texture into the terrain shader alongside the existing burn/heat mask, weighing format and filtering tradeoffs for precision. Given WebGL2's float linear filtering isn't guaranteed, I'm settling on HalfFloatType since half-float linear filtering is supported natively, with a moderate grid resolution relying on bilinear interpolation and fwidth-based anti-aliasing for smooth contour lines. For the isochrone contours I'm deriving a signed-distance-style line test from the arrival field, then wrestling with how to fake dashed line styles since there's no natural along-contour parameterization — considering screen-space or world-space checker patterns as an approximation, though diagonal artifacts are a concern. Since fire isochrones are roughly concentric around the ignition point, I realize I can use angle times radius around an origin point as a reasonable dash-length parameter, which is elegant and generalizable. I'm adding an origin field to the spec (defaulting to the field's minimum location) for this purpose, and now figuring out how to convert dash length from meters to screen pixels using the existing meters-per-pixel uniforms that roads already use for minimum width scaling. Converting that parameter to pixels using fwidth is a bit unstable and could cause shimmer when zooming, so I'm considering quantizing the dash period per zoom level like the line shader does with its scale uniform — checking how that shader computes dash periods from line distance and scale to mirror the same approach. For the PiP view, isochrones shouldn't appear since they're annotations rather than sensor data, so I'm masking those out by the sensor flag while keeping burned/heat physical overlays visible. Burn state comes from comparing arrival time to the clock, and heat intensity forms a band near the fire front using a smoothstep over the time difference, combined with the existing effects mask by taking the max of field-based and texture-based values so the glow extends slightly beyond the perimeter stroke. I'm also accounting for points just ahead of the fire front getting a pre-heating glow, defining the time-since-burned variable so heat decays exponentially behind the line but ramps up a few minutes before it arrives, with the band naturally widening in distance terms where the spread rate is faster at the head versus the heel. Now I need to figure out how the perimeter line itself, rendered as a Line2 with time-varying colors, should update as the scrub time changes. I'm realizing it's cheaper to skip regenerating the Line2 perimeter each frame and instead draw the fire edge directly in the terrain shader as a glowing emissive contour, which drapes correctly over the surface at zero extra draw calls, so I can drop the separate perimeter draw call entirely. For hotspots, I'm giving each point an optional visibility window attribute so the shader can hide or shrink points outside the current time range based on the scrub clock, keeping it cheap and letting only the active fire front show hotspots. For picking, I need burned state and a burn timestamp derived from comparing the field's time array to the current clock, then formatting that into a readable wall-clock label like "Aug 14 at 23:20" — which means the engine needs a clock epoch mapping, so I'm adding a generic `setSceneTime` call plus a `clockEpoch` option so field times can be converted to real timestamps. For structures, I'm thinking of a per-building state derived at each clock tick: destroyed if the burn-arrival time has passed, and threatened if the arrival time falls within 60 minutes ahead, matching the PRD's isochrone-based threat highlighting, with a computed count exposed through an event. I should add a `getStructureCounts()` method returning threatened, destroyed, and total so the harness can display real numbers instead of a hardcoded figure. The per-building check across roughly 1100 buildings is cheap enough to run every clock update at 60fps, and I still need to decide which buildings fall inside the new ridge-area burn zone rather than the old burn-scar polygon. For line overlays, I'm adding a `state` field supporting proposed, committed, draft, and compromised, mapped to a generic "status ladder" styling convention the engine applies automatically. For 'proposed', the line renders hollow — thin outline rails instead of a solid core, reduced glow, frozen chevrons, slightly higher opacity — while 'draft' forces amber color, thinner width, no glow, lower opacity, and a dashed pattern per the ghosted-draft convention. Forcing draft's color at the engine level rather than leaving it to scenario authors ensures drafts can never be mistaken for committed routes, which seems worth enforcing as a hard rule. For 'compromised' I'm using red with a short dash pattern and no chevrons, also forced; and for an alternate/standby route I'm leaning toward cyan dashed thin with no glow to signal "available, not active" — though I need to check it doesn't visually collide with the hollow cyan proposed style. For the D→E transition where only status changes without movement, I want the overlay rebuild to reuse identical geometry so the line itself doesn't visually jump, just its styling updates. This same state-based approach should extend to polygons too — proposed zones get dashed outlines with reduced fill opacity while committed ones show full fill/hatch, and draft polygons appear as amber ghost outlines. Markers would similarly toggle a "proposed" styling class for dashed/reduced-opacity appearance, all driven through the same layer-state mechanism rather than separate redraw logic. For crossfade transitions between phases, lines and points can animate cheaply via opacity/uniforms, and markers via CSS transitions, but polygon masks are trickier since repainting the full canvas and re-uploading the texture every frame for a transition is costly — I'm weighing whether to just skip fading polygons and let them pop in instead, since they're already low-alpha overlays anyway. I'll go simpler instead: a general `engine.batch(fn, {fadeMs})` wrapper that handles layer add/remove/tint crossfade together, with removed layers kept in a fading list that tweens opacity to zero before disposal. For opacity I'd thread uniforms through each layer type (line material, hotspot shader uniform, marker CSS), and only sample draw-call budgets after a fade settles since mid-fade counts are temporarily inflated. For unit tracks, I'm thinking positions interpolate along dense timed polylines per the scene clock, with breadcrumb trails rendered as extra small points in the same marker geometry batch to avoid added draw calls. For drones, since the scene clock can be static during standby, patrol motion needs its own animTime-based loop (a closed path) as an alternative to orbiting, so a drone can still sweep a waypoint path even while the mission timeline is paused. For the pulsing beacon marker, I'm using CSS animation for the pulse ring rather than WebGL draws, which keeps GPU cost at zero and lets the existing "is-still" class pause it when the engine parks. Camera flyTo per phase already exists, so now I'm checking the draw-call budget starting with the terrain layer. Counting draw calls across layers: terrain, ocean, roads, buildings, trees, shrubs give 6, plus overlays for routes, choke lines, hotspots, unit markers, and drone segments—since fire-perimeter moved into the shader it drops to zero draws. Adding up Phase G's route states, dozer lines, and feed layers, I land around 13-14 main calls, safely under the 20 budget, and I'm now considering keeping the draft route B line as a separate layer during revision versus merging it with the committed alignment. Now I'm sketching out a scenarioPlayer.ts module that would wrap the engine and drive playback: a factory function taking the engine and a scenario JSON (phases, layered windows, unit tracks, clock), with methods for stepping phases, scrubbing time, play/pause, emitting phase/time/plan events, and handling plan actions like authorizing transitions, proposing draft routes, and approving them. For `setActiveRoute`, I'm reasoning through the PRD's intent: swaps should behave differently depending on phase — in the proposed phase D, a route swap can modify the proposal directly since nothing's committed yet, while in later committed phases (E/F/G) a swap should instead create a draft requiring approval. I'm also planning a pure resolve function to compute the active layer state given a phase and timestamp. For scrubbing, I'm thinking through how operator decisions (route choices, drafts) need to be logged as timestamped events so resolving state at any given time only applies decisions up to that point — this satisfies the rule that scrubbing back restores the exact prior state, and scrubbing forward reapplies later decisions. I'm weighing whether making a new decision at an earlier timestamp should truncate the decision log going forward. Now I'm sketching the situation JSON schema itself — fields for metadata, an epoch-relative clock defining scene start/end minutes, and a phases array where each phase captures its id, timing, operator/talon/job context, camera, and weather state. I'm also drafting layers for optional data overlays like detection feeds with provenance and per-phase status, plus units that track entities and their per-phase gimbal/patrol/track details, and a plan section organizing named routes with a designated primary route. Phase keys like D and E are actually timeline markers rather than operator decisions -- authorization happens at E's scripted time, so pressing "Authorize" during D just jumps forward to E's timestamp. That simplifies things: phases form the scripted timeline, operator controls are shortcuts through that script, and the only real branch point is the route choice. Now I'm working out the approve/reject behavior in phase G -- approving a draft logs the decision, while rejecting removes the draft from the script. I'm also sketching the seven-phase timeline starting with Standby at T-30, and wrestling with how the displayed clock should reconcile scenario time against the day/night lighting toggle, since those seem like they could conflict. I'll settle on wall clock = epoch + elapsed time, with separate day/night epochs defined per lighting variant so the scenario can run as either a morning or pre-dawn exercise. I'll wire the PiP clock to read a label driven by this epoch setting rather than a fixed display. Now I'm sketching the phase timeline starting from first detection at T0, working backward to the Standby phase at T-20, and mapping out the terrain, roads, structures, and asset positions like FT-01's patrol sweep and the E-31/E-32 station per the doctrine reference. I'm placing E-31 and E-32 at a staging area along PCH, avoiding real station claims, with SH-12 on patrol and mutual aid units arriving later from outside the frame. Then at Detection (T+0), I'm figuring out the pulsing amber beacon marker for the unverified heat anomaly and which unit — likely FT-01 on patrol — triggers it. For phase B, FT-01 retasks to orbit the detection point with a card noting "Operator dispatched FT-01 to look (T+0:02)". On the PiP auto-open question, I'm reconciling the PRD's request for thermal-mode auto-open against doc12's "TALON never moves furniture" principle — leaning toward surfacing an "Open FT-01 IR feed" prompt rather than forcing the feed open automatically. Since my earlier proposal list didn't explicitly cover PiP, I'll add a "Director" toggle (default on) that makes camera and feed follow the script during autoplay replay, since replay is meant to be a presentation — while manual stepping leaves control with the operator. This feels like a reasonable compromise to document, and then I move to phase C sizing at T+25, where the field fire's burned area and isochrones (+15/+30) need defining. I'm weighing whether to add a head-axis line showing fire advance direction — it would add a draw call, pushing overlay counts higher later, so I'm considering rendering it as a thin dashed orange chevron arrow to fit the "advance direction" flow semantics, distinct from the cyan chevrons already used elsewhere. For weather, I'll skip adding a separate wind-vector marker on the map and instead rely on the harness telemetry strip for RAWS readout and fire danger data, keeping provenance there rather than cluttering the map with invented station positions. Moving to the triage and plan layers: I'm computing threatened structures live from the +60 isochrone field with a live count, filling the burn scar, plotting hotspot points with time windows, and then building out the D Plan at T+38 — proposed zone outlines, primary/alternate routes, choke and staging markers, and a planned dozer suppression line, still working out the right color and dash style for that line to distinguish it from active lines. Now I'm counting total draw calls across overlays and base layers to check if I'm staying under the 20-layer budget — tallying routes, choke segments, dozer line, head axis, hotspots, units, and drone segments against the base feed of terrain, roads, buildings, trees, and hotspots. It's landing right at 20, which is risky, so I'm considering merging the choke marker into the route line or dropping the head axis in later phases to leave some margin. For the gated-action trigger, I need the harness to show an "Authorize plan" button with an expiry countdown, tied to the principle that silence never counts as approval. A real-time countdown feels wrong for a replay, so I'm leaning toward expressing the expiry as a scenario-time deadline instead. Then for phase E, authorization locks in at T+44 with an authority marker at Zone 1's centroid, and the zone gets a hatched fill to show the order is committed. Phase F covers operations from T+50 to T+95, tracking units like E-31, E-32, and DZ-3 as they move toward Zone 1 and along the dozer suppression line. I'm also working out route status logic — Route A should flip to "compromised" automatically once the fire's arrival time at any route point falls within 10 minutes of the current time, driven by live field data rather than a fixed keyframe. Alongside this, evac clearing percentage chips show progress labels like "ZONE 1 · 68% CLEARED." For the revision pass around T+70, Route A becomes compromised as fire crosses it, so TALON drafts Route B as the new primary (shown as an amber ghost line) until the operator approves it, switching it to committed cyan chevrons while Route A stays marked red. I also need to check the fire timing holds up — tracing arrival time per cell from ignition outward, treating the final egg-shaped perimeter as a self-similar scaling around the ignition point so each location's arrival fraction is the smallest scale factor at which it falls inside the growing boundary. That confirms the heel sits approximately at I, so the ring stays star-shaped despite noise. I'm now considering a more credible approach: using a Dijkstra/fast-marching arrival-time simulation over the DEM grid with slope and wind-dependent elliptical rate-of-spread, leveraging real terrain and fuel data for a more physically grounded fire model. But since the user wants to keep the current built map and scenario, switching to Dijkstra would alter the existing egg-shaped perimeter's look, so I'll stick with the self-similar field approach, defining f(p) as distance from ignition scaled by directional radius, and deriving arrival time from that so the final perimeter exactly matches the current state. I'm also considering whether the TALON isochrones should just be the same field evaluated at future offsets, implying a perfect model — reasonable for a training script if projections are continuously re-run. For the travel route, I'm routing DZ-3 east on PCH, up Trancas Canyon Rd to its top, then cross-country to the dozer line start, moving at about 25 m/min along the contingency line. Labeling it "DZ-3 · Dozer · Contingency line · south flank" before moving on to the next asset, FT-01. FT-01 needs a multi-phase track: a patrol sweep across the canyon, then transitioning into an orbit over the detection point by T+4, then orbiting the fire head, then settling into overwatch with gimbal locked on HS-01. Each phase needs its own gimbal target since the detection point and fire head move independently over time, with a thermal overlay spec at 980°C. I'm also checking whether ground crews like E-31/E-32/SH-12 should be staged at standby positions, possibly near LACoFD Station 71/72 in the area. Since I don't want to fabricate a real station, I'll describe the standby position generically as "Available · PCH patrol" rather than naming a specific station. For the weather keyframes, I'm labeling the A phase (T−30) with wind, humidity, temperature, and a Red Flag Warning, sourcing it generically as simulated RAWS data since this fire scenario is fictional. Since both the weather and detections are authored for this exercise, I'm tagging their provenance as "authored (exercise)" in reality, while keeping the in-scenario product semantics showing them as "measured" (e.g., FT-01 LWIR) within the simulated world, trusting the harness banner to flag it as an exercise overall. Now I'm drafting the escalating weather progression across keyframes — A starts elevated (ENE 14 mph gusting 24, RH 12%, 81°F, Red Flag), moving toward C which intensifies further (ENE 22 mph gusting 38, RH 8%, 86°F, Critical status). I'm also building out the wind marker and detection sequence: a rotated arrow indicator tracking wind direction toward 247°, matching fire spread WSW; detection text escalating from unconfirmed heat (71% confidence) to confirmed active flame at 412°C, with a hotter 980°C pixel reading appearing once the picture-in-picture locks onto HS-01. Burned acreage is computed per phase card as a modeled value tied to the clock. For the smaller incident scenario, I'm placing it near 34.048N 118.868W with its own phase timeline—standby, detection, then operations with E-32 and crew C-5 staging on the nearest road plus a drone orbit—and a short hand line perimeter around 120 m, keeping the map sparse with no routes or zones and a tighter camera zoom. I'm confirming standby.json should be its own Phase-A-only file per doc12's three-file structure, and that the procedural harness should let a legacy demo scenario be wrapped as a single-phase "Snapshot" situation so it flows through the same player without a clock. I'm also noting the engine's built-in demo scenario logic is incident-specific and needs to stay separate from this new procedural flow per doc12. Now I'm wrestling with where buildDemoScenario actually belongs — it's fixture-generation code sitting inside terrainEngine.ts, which the PRD wants to be a pure, incident-agnostic engine, so having it there technically violates that boundary. I'm weighing whether to extract it into a separate fixtures.ts, but that creates import dependencies back into terrainEngine for things like Heightfield, which complicates the build.mjs inlining step for the file:// fallback case. I realize I could rewrite the import specifier at runtime, swapping './terrainEngine.js' for the engine's blob URL before importing the fixtures source, which would actually work. But buildDemoScenario leans on a bunch of private helpers I'd need to export, which feels like too much surgery for now — and I'm noticing the engine's applyScenario method itself branches on scenario type, which conflicts with the acceptance criteria that no engine code should branch on incident type. So I'm leaning toward a real tier separation: pulling the fire/incident fixtures (FireRun, simulateFireRun, DemoScenario, buildDemoScenario) out into their own module, maybe scenarioFixtures.ts, to keep the engine incident-agnostic as the spec demands. I'm also mapping which utility exports stay with the core engine (math/geometry helpers, palette, Heightfield, RoadNetwork) versus removing the engine's auto-demo scenario handling entirely — treating that as a documented breaking change, since the burn-scar/progression logic in pick() is fire-specific and belongs with the fixtures, not the core. I need to split things into separate files: a generic terrainEngine, a scenarioFixtures module for the procedural demo fire logic, and a scenarioPlayer for tier 2 runtime, updating imports like the encinal-scenario tool accordingly. I'm working through how the build script should inline these as separate blobs and how tsc will emit the import statements between them. My plan is to first rework the engine, then move scenarioFixtures and scenarioPlayer, update the scenario tool to output JSON files for each scenario, then adjust the harness, build script, verification, and README. Before writing code I still need to review the remaining engine sections — world loading, event binding, CSS, type declarations, and the HUD update logic — so I'm going to look at those next.

Route B is confirmed as the north leg up Encinal toward Mulholland, since PCH east isn't a viable exit for residents above the fire's start point on Encinal Canyon Rd. Next, I'll review the engine's event, CSS, and world-loading code before making edits.

I'm setting up a shared field system with a texture-based uniform group and a GLSL helper function that computes burn and heat values from position, to be reused across the terrain fragment and vegetation vertex shaders. For the terrain fragment I need anti-aliased burn edges using fwidth-based smoothstep, computed separately from the shared function. I'm also working out texture coordinate mapping so that row 0 (north) aligns correctly with the vertical axis, deciding to flip the v-coordinate in the shader rather than reversing rows on upload, keeping the tiling cell-centered to match vegetation sampling. I'm using half-float data with a sentinel "never" value of 60000, but I realize this creates a problem: the huge jump from normal field values (like 300) to the sentinel causes extreme gradients in fwidth, which could produce spurious contour lines along that boundary. I need to make sure field values extend continuously beyond the scenario rather than jumping discontinuously to the sentinel. So instead of a hard sentinel, I'll compute the field as distance divided by a floored radius (keeping R at least 60m) so it stays continuous everywhere, even near the heel where R approaches zero. As a backup safeguard, the shader can also suppress contour lines wherever fwidth exceeds a threshold, filtering out any remaining spurious edges. For buildings, I'm combining the bilinear-sampled field burn/heat with the legacy polygon-based values by taking the max of both, and for vegetation I'm applying the same field texture lookup in the vertex shader, merging it with the existing fx.r/fx.g channels. I'll add uClock and uTintFade to shared uniforms, and extend the terrain material with field uniforms plus uTintPrev, uTintFade, and uScale, then move on to the GLSL shader edits.
Now I'm adding a GLSL field chunk for time-of-arrival data per engine, sampling an arrival texture with clock-based fade and edge width parameters. I'm figuring out the texture row orientation so arrival data lines up correctly with the terrain's north-south axis, since the data texture isn't flipped vertically. Now I'm writing the terrain fragment shader logic that computes burn and heat fields from the arrival texture — using fwidth to detect discontinuities, smoothstep to create soft fronts, and exponential decay for heat falloff after the fire passes. The burn value feeds into char mixing and heat drives glow and ember effects later in the shader. I need to insert this arrival-field code right before the char mix step, but draw the isochrone contour lines afterward so they render on top of graticules. For rate-of-spread, I'm working out how to approximate the gradient of the arrival time using screen-space derivatives relative to texel size, so I can derive spread rate in distance-per-time and use it to brighten the fire's leading edge. Now I'm setting up the intensity falloff, edge highlighting for the fire perimeter, and starting to define isochrone contour uniforms for toggling offsets and colors. Writing dash-pattern shader logic... I need to declare this function before main in the shader. There's a minor seam glitch at the atan discontinuity that's acceptable, and I want isochrones to only appear ahead of the front, hidden under sensor mode, with colors kept simple rather than adding extra casing for legibility. For the vegetation vertex shader, I'm wiring in the field burn logic so it shares the same arrival-time uniforms as the terrain, computing burn and heat values from the arrival data to drive vHeat and burnt state, and setting up a shared field uniforms object to pass those values through. I'm also planning to add window-attribute culling to the hotspot shader for offscreen points and opacity fades, plus a uHollow uniform for the line fragment shader. For the hollow line effect, the core becomes transparent in the middle so only the rails and chevrons show, with glow reduced accordingly while frozen via uSpeed=0. For the marker fragment shader, I'm adding a trail-dot shape with per-vertex alpha so trailing dots fade without the dark ring outline. Now I'm working out how draped lines get drawn into the paint masks, converting a line's width parameter into meters at the mask's resolution so dozer lines render at a sensible physical width, with dashing also specified in meters. For polygon states, proposed polygons get a dashed outline with low-alpha fill. I'm layering in a tint crossfade between a previous and current texture, blended by a fade uniform so terrain color transitions smoothly over time. For isochrone field labels, I'm computing each label's screen position by marching along a ray from its origin toward a target direction, bilinearly sampling the field on the CPU to find where the value matches the label's clock offset, then updating the label element's position whenever the clock changes. Now I'm writing the fade-out and layer-swap logic for setOverlayLayer, handling optional fade duration by either fading or removing the existing layer before building the new one with fade state tracked in its record. Fading-out layers go into a separate tracking list with a tween, disposing objects once complete; polygons crossfade via mask repaint while field layers just pop since their fades rarely matter visually. I'm defining applyLayerOpacity to handle opacity differently per layer type—scaling line material opacity by a stored base value, setting a shader uniform for points, and directly setting CSS opacity for DOM elements. For the tint crossfade, I'm tracking a fade request flag that triggers copying the current tint canvas to a "previous" canvas before clearing, then tweening a fade uniform from 0 to 1. There's a subtlety where if multiple polygon changes batch together before a repaint, only one copy happens at the first paint, which works fine—though if a fade is mid-flight when another change arrives, the previous copy captures the already-updated canvas, causing a minor visual jump that's acceptable. Fading-out layers are also excluded from the mask repaint since they're removed from the active layers list. Now I'm designing `setLayerState` to update a layer's spec and, for line layers, recompute material uniforms (color, style, dash, speed, glow, hollow, linewidth) via a `lineUniformValues` helper, with linewidth being just a uniform change rather than a geometry rebuild—so I'll write a `styleLine` function that resolves all these style properties into one object. For other layer types, polygons mark the mask dirty, markers toggle a CSS state class, and fields are unaffected by state changes. I'm also working out hit-testing: `pickLayer` iterates visible interactive layers in reverse order, projecting resampled line points to screen space to find the nearest segment, or checking marker bounding rects, and click events only fire when pointer movement and duration stay under small thresholds, emitting a `layerclick` event with the hit id. Now I'm thinking through marker DOM interactivity, making layer containers non-interactive by default but enabling pointer events on individual marker elements so they can catch clicks and forward them as `layerclick`. For line projection I convert world coordinates (including elevation exaggeration and lift) into screen space using the active camera. For units, I'm defining how ground position is derived — from a track interpolation, a patrol path, or a static spec position — and how drone position builds on a moving center (track, patrol, or orbit) plus altitude computation for orbiting behavior. Now I need altitude to track terrain height at the drone's current center rather than a fixed point, so instead of storing a fixed MSL altitude I should store AGL and resample ground height at the live center each frame, letting the drone bob naturally over varying terrain in a smoothed way. I'm also noticing a bug where patrol drones without an explicit gimbal target would look straight down at their own position, causing the lookAt up-vector to degenerate into NaN since it's parallel to the view direction — I need to give patrol drones a sensible default gaze target ahead of their motion instead. For that fix, I'll make drones without a gimbal target look roughly 300 meters ahead along their current heading, falling back to north if no heading is defined. Separately, I'm planning out trail breadcrumbs for tracked units — placing fading dot markers at fixed time intervals behind the current position, which means extending the marker points geometry with extra trail slots and an alpha attribute so older dots fade, then wiring this into the position update and rebuild logic, while also sorting out which units should be considered continuously animated versus driven purely by the scene clock. For each layer active at time t, I resolve its spec by merging patches applied up to that point, determining state from the most recent keyframe or falling back to spec/committed defaults, and applying role styles for routed layers before outputting with provenance info. I compute a lightweight signature for each layer (patch index, role, draft flag) instead of stringifying the full spec, so I can detect state-only changes versus structural changes cheaply and decide whether to call setLayerState or rebuild via setOverlayLayer — this avoids expensive JSON comparisons on large field data. Units get similar signature-based change detection using ids and patch indices, though since their spec objects contain large track arrays, any detected change triggers a full setUnits rebuild. I'm now working out the fire perimeter layer itself: it shouldn't render until the fire is "sized" per doc12's rule that no perimeter exists until sizing completes, so the field activates from the sizing phase onward with a burn scar fill, a fire-colored edge, and isochrone rings at +15 and +30 minutes — still deciding on colors to avoid clashing with the amber detection tones, leaning toward solid fire-orange for +15 and a lighter dashed shade for +30. Then I hit a structural snag: the fire perimeter and isochrones are meant to toggle independently in the harness UI, but the engine only supports one field per layer, so grouping them into a single "fire" layer means I can't offer separate toggles unless I either split them into two synced layers or have the harness re-issue the field spec with isochrones stripped out when toggled off. Now I'm adding a wind marker positioned ahead of the head, rotated toward WSW with labels showing wind speed/gusts and relative humidity, sourced from a simulated RAWS feed, plus deciding how the ignition marker should replace the detection marker once the fire grows past phase C. For the evacuation plan, I'm setting up zone polygons (order, warning, safe) with distinct colors and states that shift from proposed to committed, computed from the fire's ring distances. I'm also removing structure threat indicators from these zone polygons since that conflicts with the field-based triage semantic, and I'm starting to define an interactive route overlay for route-a. Now I'm adding route-b along Encinal, defining shared route styling (primary solid cyan with glow/chevron animation, alternate dashed cyan), and setting up the choke point at Encinal's hairpin turn with its marker detail — noting the SH-12 traffic control mention should only appear starting at phase F, patched in later. For the transition logic, I'm setting the track to move from the drone's current patrol position to an orbit point near the detection over four minutes, accepting the visual jump since it happens during a fade. I'm patching in orbit radius changes, gimbal targeting toward the detection and then the head standoff point, and temperature confirmation values at specific checkpoints, plus positioning for the existing stand at a later patch point. Now I'm working through how the fire head's position changes over time from C onward, trying to compute a standoff point west-southwest of the moving head at five-minute intervals, but running into the problem that gimbal target is a static field that would need a patch at every interval to track a moving target. I'm leaning toward patching the gimbal target every 10 scene minutes instead of 5, since that's close enough to follow the head's movement without excessive rebuilds, while using continuous track motion for the drone's orbit center itself. Now I'm working out E-31's positioning: it starts standing by near the PCH junction west, then tracks a drive up Encinal to its structure protection spot at a specific point along the route. For E-32, I'm placing it on standby near Trancas Canyon Rd on PCH, then routing it to Trancas Top for structure protection duty there. SH-12 (law enforcement) stays on PCH patrol east of the junction before executing the evacuation order and tracking to the hairpin for traffic control, while DZ-3 the dozer enters as mutual aid from the east frame edge. I'm now working out the dozer's movement — driving PCH west, turning up Trancas Canyon Rd, then following the dozer line cross-country at a slower pace, confirming E-31, E-32, DZ-3, and SH-12 all start present on the roads per the scenario requirements. Now I'm putting together the final summary: noting the Route B deviation from PCH east to Encinal north, the timeline and draw call values, moving setPhase/setActiveRoute into the player rather than the engine, the director's auto-PiP option, and the breaking change of fixtures moving out so the engine no longer auto-applies the demo scenario (removing the `scenario` option) while keeping scenario.json. I also want to flag triangles still around 416k, fire spread being self-similar rather than Rothermel-based, and include the run commands — all kept concise.

The incident flow is now part of the system as a third tier. You can step or scrub through all 7 phases from standby to plan revision on the real Encinal data, and the headless check passes 29/29.

Three tiers

  • terrainEngine.ts is now incident-agnostic. The fire simulation and procedural demo moved out to a new scenarioFixtures.ts. Breaking change: the engine no longer applies the demo on its own, so the old scenario option is gone.
  • data/scenarios/*.json holds the three situations from doc 12: standby, small-incident and wui-breakout. tools/encinal-scenario.mjs generates them from the real roads, terrain and buildings.
  • scenarioPlayer.ts is new and plays a situation file on the engine. setPhase, next/prev, scrubbing, autoplay and setActiveRoute live here, not in the engine, as we agreed.
  • harness.html now opens on the WUI breakout at Standby. It has a situation selector, a phase card with Authorize / Approve / Reject, a telemetry block marked measured / modeled / authored, and the timeline bar along the bottom: Prev, the phase buttons, Next, Auto-play, plus a time scrubber.

The arc (minutes from first detection)

PhaseTimeWhat appears
A StandbyT−0:30FT-01 on a sweep, units available, Red Flag weather
B DetectionT+0:00One pulsing point, confirmed at T+0:06; FT-01 retasked with the IR feed
C SizingT+0:20Burned area, flame front, +15/+30/+60 min isochrones, wind, structure triage
D PlanT+0:38The whole plan in "proposed" styling, plus the gated evacuation order with its expiry time
E AuthorizedT+0:46The same plan restyled as committed; no geometry is rebuilt
F OperationsT+0:54Units drive real roads with breadcrumb trails; mutual-aid dozer DZ-3 arrives
G RevisionT+1:39Projected cut of Encinal Canyon Rd; draft of Route B next to the committed plan

Rules from doc 12 that are now enforced

  • A draft can never look committed. The engine owns the status styling, so no scenario data can override it. A draft is ghosted amber, thinner and dashed; "proposed" lines are hollow with frozen chevrons.
  • Route swap. Clicking a route, or calling player.setActiveRoute(), edits the proposal before authorization. After authorization it stages a draft you must approve or reject.
  • Time is deterministic. Scrubbing back restores the earlier state exactly; the check confirms this.
  • No hard-coded counts. Burned acreage and threatened structures are computed from the fire projection, not typed in.
  • Small incident stays small. It only ever has the detection and a hand line, never a perimeter.

Draw calls stay within 20 in every phase with the drone feed open. The worst case is G at 14 + 5 = 19. Phases A and B are 8 + 4, C is 10 + 5, D to F are 12 + 5. The isochrones, zones, dozer line and breadcrumbs cost no extra draw calls. With motion off, nothing renders at all (0 frames).

Decisions for you

  • Route B is now Encinal Canyon Rd north toward Mulholland, not PCH east as I had proposed. The projection reaches Encinal Canyon Rd at T+2:09. The data shows the only way out for the 19 structures above that point is north, so PCH east can't help them. The catch: Route B is the upper part of Route A's road, so in phase G several styles stack on one stretch. Choosing a different corridor would mean picking a different fire.
  • Auto-opening the drone feed in phase B is behind a "Follow phase" toggle, on by default. This keeps the PRD behaviour while letting the operator turn it off, which doc 12's "TALON never moves furniture" asks for. Your call which way the default should go.
  • The fire spread is a simple growth of the existing perimeter shape, not a real fire-behaviour model. The README and the provenance labels say so. A real model is a natural next layer.

Still open: triangles remain about 416k with vegetation, and data/scenario.json is kept as the old single-state snapshot.

To run: npm run serve, then open http://127.0.0.1:8130/harness.html. npm run verify runs the checks, and npm run phases saves a screenshot of every phase to qa/ and prints draw calls.

"This OS" is probably referring to the product itself—likely the TALON/Sentinel command platform built as an operating system for incident command. I should pull together what I've gathered from the docs like DECISIONS.md and SPEC.md, touching on things like the command deck, composition targets, fidelities, and the degradation ladder, while being clear about what's directly documented versus what I'm inferring. My core theory: Sentinel's kernel is a shared, provenance-tracked world-state model, with the map as just one rendering of that state—TALON can only propose drafts while humans retain commit authority, and every action expires rather than staying silently approved. It maps closely to version control concepts (committed plan as HEAD, drafts as branches, approvals as merges, time-scrubbing as checkout), with layers functioning like permissioned files and the whitelisted composition targets acting as a constrained UI/syscall surface—proof that this is meant to be a general-purpose kernel rather than a fire-specific app. The real gap in my build is that it's script-driven rather than event-sourced: a proper implementation would treat the situation as a log of events from multiple sources (drones, weather, TALON, operator) with the map as a fold over that log, which my scenario player already half-approximates. I still need to make decisions/events first-class, add expiring operator authority, finish the interrogation rule, and build the fidelity ladder—and I should flag that "OS" might actually imply multiple coexisting surfaces (command deck, fleet roster, comms) beyond just the map, which I could ask about directly.

I don't think the product is a fire map. I think it's an operating system for incident command, and the map is just one screen on it. Here is my theory, built from the two docs and from building against them. I've only seen DECISIONS.md, SPEC.md and the command deck referenced, never read them, so parts of this are inference.

1. The core is a shared record of what is true and what is proposed.
Doc 12's first line, "the map is a function of (situation state, time)", is the centre of the design. Everything else (map, drone feed, telemetry, the deck) is a different view of that one record. That is why the engine must know nothing about fire. A screen that has opinions about the content can't serve more than one kind of incident.

2. Authority works like version control.

  • The committed plan is the current approved version.
  • A TALON draft is a proposed change against it.
  • Approve means merge. Reject means discard.
  • Scrubbing time is like checking out an earlier state, and it must be exact.
  • "Silence is never approval" means a gated action expires instead of applying itself.

The most important visual rule ("a draft must never be mistakable for a commitment") is really this rule shown on screen. The operator has to see the difference between the approved plan and the proposal, not just two plans.

3. TALON is a guest with limited powers, not the one running things.
It can propose content (projections, plans, drafts, which layers should exist). It can't commit anything, and it can't rearrange the screen ("TALON never moves furniture; composition targets are whitelisted"). The operator holds commit authority and control of the screen. The situation holds the facts. So the design is built around who owns what, and doc 12's "Owner" column is a set of access rights.

4. Provenance is part of every fact.
Measured, modeled and authored aren't decoration. Every value carries its source, the same way data carries a type. "Omitted, not faked" follows from this: a layer you can't source doesn't exist.

5. Standby and the small incident are the real tests.
Anyone can make a wildfire look dramatic. A calm standby map and a genuinely small incident show the system is general-purpose rather than one hard-coded scenario. I suspect the "three fidelities and degradation ladder" in SPEC.md is the same idea applied to bandwidth and hardware.

How the current build lines up

  • Closest match: the player already computes state from the situation, the time and the decisions, and the engine enforces the status styling.
  • Still script-driven: a real system would build the situation from a stream of events coming from drones, weather, TALON and the operator. Right now the player plays a scripted timeline.
  • Missing:
    • interrogation (doc 12's rule 6, "what is this, where from, how fresh, who owns it") is only partly done;
    • expiry on gated actions is cosmetic;
    • nothing of the fidelity ladder exists.

Where I might be wrong

  • I'm assuming "OS" means a single system with several screens (map, deck, fleet roster, comms) that all read the same state. If the map is actually meant to be the whole product, point 1 overreaches.
  • I'm treating the charter as the demo story and doc 12 as the real contract. If the cinematic demo is the actual goal right now, the priorities flip.

Does this match how you think about it? If it does, the next layer I'd build is turning decisions and detections into a real event log the player reads from, rather than a fixed script.
