ThinkingTime to finalize the answer, tightening it up a bit from the draft.
Time to finalize the answer, tightening it up a bit from the draft.

Yes, the idea is possible as a concept. Most of the pieces already exist in the real world, just separately. What nobody has solved well is how an AI and a human share authority in a crisis, and that is exactly the part a designer should own. That's your case study.

If I were TALON, this is the power I'd want

My rule: my power should depend on how easy an action is to undo and how many people it affects. It shouldn't depend on how confident I am, because I can be confidently wrong.

PowerDo it alone?Why
Read every feed, sensor and recordYesSeeing more costs nobody anything
Run and re-run models, draft plans before anyone asksYesCheap, easy to undo, and where I'm genuinely faster
Send a drone to lookYes, inside a pre-cleared airspace box, and I announce itLooking can be undone; airspace shared with air tankers isn't my call
Send the standard first response to a confirmed detectionYes, if a pre-approved response plan covers itDispatch already works like this; the authority was granted in advance
Escalate: raise the incident level, call in outside helpRecommend; the operator decidesIt commits people and money
Evacuation zones, routes, public alertsPrepare all of it; the operator (and the legal authority) decidesIt lands on people who never chose me
Change what's highlighted or which panel is in frontYes, announced, and never over something the operator pinnedI can guide attention; the screen belongs to the operator
Hide or remove dataNeverIf I can hide things, I can be wrong without anyone seeing
Override the operatorNever; I escalate to a second human insteadA person has to be accountable

Two more powers I'd ask for that people usually forget:

  • A loud "I don't know." When a feed is out of date, or the drone disagrees with my model, I'd say so right next to the recommendation, not in a footnote.
  • An approved way to disagree. Say the operator sends engine E-31 down a road I predict will close in 12 minutes. I'd say so once, with the evidence, on the record. If they still say go, it goes.

Your concept already matches how real fire agencies work

  • TALON is an AI version of an existing job. US fire agencies use the Incident Command System (ICS). In it, a planning team prepares the plan for the incident and the incident commander approves it. That team tracks what's happening, where every unit is, and the written record, and includes a fire behaviour specialist. You're not inventing a new chain of command; you're making an existing role fast. That sentence alone makes the concept credible to people in the field.
  • Your "levels" already exist. Incidents are rated from Type 5 (smallest) to Type 1 (most complex). TALON recommending a type at the end of sizing links the two situations we built. The small incident is roughly the Type 4–5 path, and the canyon breakout escalates toward Type 1–2.
  • Research gives you the vocabulary. Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens (2000) split automation into four stages: gather information, analyse it, choose an action, carry it out. Each stage gets its own level of independence. That is the table above. Cite it; it's the backbone of your authority model.

Two places I'd push back

1. TALON can guide attention, but should never hide data. Let it bring a panel forward, highlight what changed, or put together a briefing view. But panels that move on their own during a crisis ruin the operator's sense of where things are. That's why your doc 12 says "TALON never moves furniture." Your doc already has most of the answer: TALON only places things in pre-approved spots. I'd add two rules:

  • anything the operator pins is off-limits to TALON;
  • every change TALON makes answers the three questions pilots famously asked about early cockpit automation: what is it doing, why did it do that, and what will it do next?

2. Don't let the operator become a rubber stamp. You said the human commands rather than just checks. I agree, and the design has to make that true. If the flow is "AI makes a plan, human clicks approve", people slide into approving whatever is put in front of them. This is called automation bias. Flip the order:

  • TALON first asks what the operator wants to prioritise, e.g. "protect the 19 homes above the road cut, or keep Route A open for crews?"
  • Then it plans within that.
  • Then it asks for approval.

The military calls this "commander's intent".

The check also works the other way. During the January 2025 LA fires, an evacuation alert meant for one area went to phones across the whole county. Imagine TALON asking: "This alert reaches the entire county; the zone you drew holds about 2,000 people. Confirm?" That protects the operator from a slip.

Is it actually possible?

As a prototype, yes, and you're most of the way there. In the real world the pieces exist separately:

  • AI smoke detection on camera networks (ALERTCalifornia, Pano AI)
  • satellites built to spot fires (FireSat)
  • fire spread prediction (Technosylva, used by CAL FIRE)
  • evacuation zone systems (Genasys Protect)
  • public alert apps (Watch Duty)

No copilot joins them up yet. The hard parts in reality aren't the AI:

  • different agencies' systems don't talk to each other;
  • phone networks go down when the cell towers burn;
  • legal authority is split between agencies (evacuation orders usually come from the police or sheriff, not the fire service);
  • spread models struggle with embers carried far ahead by the wind.

Two things worth saying in your case study:

  • TALON isn't one model. It's a language model that coordinates specialist models for detection, fire spread and traffic. It directs the fire scientist rather than being one.
  • The prototype doesn't need the real model. A believable simulation labelled "modeled" is honest. Showing its uncertainty as a band, rather than one crisp line, is a stronger design moment than fake precision.

What I'd build next, in order

  1. Make TALON visible. Right now TALON is just a script, and plans simply appear. Add a proposal card showing:

    • what it proposes;
    • why (tap it and the evidence lights up on the map);
    • how confident it is, and the deadline;
    • Approve, Edit, Reject and Ask why buttons.

    This becomes your hero screen.

  2. Show options on the map. At the planning step, TALON offers two or three options, each drawn in the existing draft style. A comparison strip shows, for each one:

    • the time to clear the zone;
    • how many crews are exposed;
    • how many homes are still in the fire's projected path.

    The operator picks one, edits it and approves it.

  3. An activity log, which gives you the replay almost for free. The map already depends only on the situation, the time and the decisions made. So the timeline scrubber we built is already a replay engine. Record every event, every recommendation (including rejected ones) and every operator action in a log that can't be edited. The post-incident review then lets you:

    • jump to each decision;
    • see exactly what the operator saw at that moment;
    • overlay what actually happened;
    • score TALON's predictions against reality.

  4. Standby isn't idle. Doc 12 says TALON is idle in standby; I'd change that. The biggest time saving isn't faster computing during the fire, it's having the plan before the fire starts. On a high-fire-danger morning, TALON prepares evacuation plans for each zone in advance and suggests where to position crews. When a detection comes in, the plan is mostly pulled up, not built from scratch.

  5. One moment where TALON is wrong. The drone sees the fire cross the road 14 minutes before the model said it would. TALON flags its own prediction, re-routes, and says so openly. The most convincing screen in any AI case study is the one where the AI fails gracefully.

What I'd stop: polishing the 3D engine. The map is good enough. Graphics performance won't get you hired; the authority model will.

For getting hired

  • The wildfire is the stage; the real skill is designing how people hand work to AI. Every team building AI agents is stuck on the same questions:

    • what can the agent do alone;
    • how does it propose;
    • how does a human edit or approve;
    • how do you tell a draft from a final decision;
    • how do you review it afterwards.

    Say that explicitly. A fintech or developer-tools team will then see their own product in your work.

  • Lead with doc 12, not the 3D. "Omitted, not faked", "Phase D→E is a state change, not a redraw" and "a draft is never mistakable for a commitment" are senior-level product rules. Put the rules and your reasoning first.

  • Be open that you built it with an AI agent. In 2026 that counts as a skill. But interviewers will dig into your decisions, so you need to explain every one. I'm glad to walk you through how the build works in plain language until you can explain it on a whiteboard.

  • Talk to one real person. A 30-minute call with a dispatcher, firefighter or emergency manager will set you apart from every generic "AI dashboard" concept. So will reading the public post-incident reviews of the 2018 Woolsey Fire (in these same Malibu mountains) and the January 2025 LA fires.

  • Ship something narrow and finished. Put a two-minute video first, because recruiters won't wait for a 3D demo to load. Then the case study, then the live link. One finished story beats a ten-feature vision.

Two questions back to you:

  1. Who exactly is the operator: a dispatcher at a command centre, the incident commander in the field, or a county emergency manager? Each has different authority, which changes what TALON can ask of them.
  2. Are you aiming at AI product roles in general, or emergency and government tech specifically? That decides how to frame the case study.

If you want to keep building, next I'd do items 1 and 3: the proposal card, and the activity log with a replay view. I can also turn the power table into a page you can drop into the case study.

ThinkingNow I need to dig into the existing harness.html file — it's massive at over 6600 lines, mostly inline compiled modules, so I want to locate the actual UI code and engine API by searching through its structure.
I'm parsing the brief for designing an operator's command center interface for autonomous drone emergency response, focusing on how the AI-native interface must collapse decision time while avoiding cognitive overload, false confidence, or loss of control. I'm noting the specific scenario details—a 3:47 AM thermal detection event with 18 mph winds pushing northeast—as grounding context for the design. I'm mapping out the 90-second detection-to-action timeline: thermal detection, AI validation and autonomous dispatch, drone airborne with operator alert, live feed confirmation of fire proximity to homes, deployment of additional drones for perimeter and evacuation support, fire department receiving GPS and routing data, and evacuation alerts going out to dozens of households in the projected fire path. Now I'm thinking through the operator's experience managing multiple zones and drones simultaneously, needing to quickly judge urgency, decide whether to trust the autonomous response or escalate, and coordinate drones, crews, and residents without feeling overwhelmed. I'm also considering the design implications — information architecture, interaction patterns, visual language, and how the AI adapts the interface — plus the creative freedom around what the operator sees and hears, how drones are coordinated without separate controls, and what makes this feel distinctly "AI-native" while reflecting FlytBase's brand as a serious, autonomous, enterprise-grade aviation platform. There's a real tension between the brand brief calling for "not playful, mission-critical" and the desire for a cute TALON mascot — I'm resolving this by keeping the FlytBase logo restrained and enterprise-grade while giving TALON a calm, minimalist personality, like a geometric eyes glyph or a stylized bird-of-prey head with precise eye slits, rather than anything cartoonish. I want to flag this reasoning to the user as I design it. I'm also expanding the scenario beyond a single drone — since the brief mentions docks and multi-drone coordination, I'll introduce FT-01 (scout/patrol), FT-02 (perimeter mapping), and FT-03 (evacuation guidance with speaker/lights), all dispatched from docks, with TALON assigning each a role so the operator isn't juggling separate controls. This connects nicely to the One model's subagent concept: instead of manual stick control, the operator approves missions while TALON allocates drones based on intent ("cover the perimeter"). I'm wondering whether the status dots should represent TALON's own software agents (Recon, Spread, Route, Notify) or the physical drones themselves, or possibly both as separate groupings. On communication design, I'm establishing a clear rule: TALON stays silent unless something genuinely needs the operator, with escalating attention tiers from a silent ledger log, to a quiet feed entry, to an amber "needs you" inbox item, up to a full interrupt with chime and map focus — reserved only for life-safety critical events. For interaction patterns, I'm planning number keys for quick inbox answers, keyboard shortcuts like command-K, space, and arrow keys, plus a push-to-talk mic button for voice input. For ground team communication, I'm designing a "Send to crews" action where TALON packages GPS coordinates, thermal maps, wind data, and approach routes for responders. I like repurposing One's "@agent" messaging pattern here — an operator typing "@SH-12 hold the hairpin" gets confirmation that the message was sent to the sheriff unit via radio-to-text, directly mirroring that established interaction model for ground teams. Now checking the epoch timestamps: January in California is PST, not PDT, so I should correct that mismatch and consider aligning the night scenario's T+0:00 to 03:47 AM as a nod to the original brief's detection time. But the wind direction conflicts — Santa Ana winds blow southwest, while the brief specifies 18 mph pushing northeast, so changing it would force re-simulating the entire fire spread and cascade through cuts, routes, and structures. That's too disruptive to the existing site-specific story, so I'll leave the wind direction as is. Still, I can cheaply align the time: the brief's atmospheric 3:47 AM detail is worth matching, so I'll adjust the night epoch to 03:47 and shift the date to January 2026/PST, keeping the daytime variant unchanged, while checking how the generator's EPOCH settings are configured. On numbers, the brief's "47 households" shouldn't be hard-coded into my scenario—I should let the actual computed count of threatened structures stand on its own rather than forcing it to match. More importantly, I'm noticing the brief's "90 seconds from detection to action" doesn't line up with my timeline, where authorization lands around T+0:46 minutes rather than under two minutes—that's a real discrepancy I need to reconcile, since my current scenario seems to represent the "old way" rather than the new faster response the brief describes. For an AI-native system the whole point is collapsing that response time, but realistically a fire needs to grow before it threatens structures. In the brief's version, the fire is already 50 meters from homes at detection, making evacuation urgent immediately, so I'm reconsidering whether my plan timing at T+0:38 makes sense or whether an AI-native proposal could come much sooner once the fire growth curve shows a threat emerging. Let me rework the timeline to reflect AI-speed response while staying physically plausible: standby readiness at T−0:30, detection at T+0:00 via sensor array triggering auto-dispatch of the nearest drone within seconds since reconnaissance is low-risk, airborne by T+0:01, on scene by T+0:03 with IR confirmation shortly after, then sizing kicks in around T+0:06 as the spread model runs isochrones and checks which structures fall in the projected path. By T+0:08 TALON proposes a plan adapted from a pre-computed playbook, authorization follows around T+0:10 with operator approval and sheriff sign-off plus alerts to affected households, and operations begin shortly after with units moving and drones guiding evacuation. The key insight is that since the fire is still small at T+0:10 (only 20 minutes old), early evacuation buys crucial time before the fire reaches homes around T+0:50–1:30 — this is what makes the difference between contained and catastrophic, and it sets up the later revision moment where the model proves wrong but the early start still saves most of the zone. I also need to adjust generator timing logic — phase times, unit dispatch and arrival calculations, gate expiry, and verification checks — so that earlier dispatch produces earlier arrivals consistently throughout the scenario file. I'm also considering adding drone dock infrastructure (Encinal dock, Zuma dock) with standby aircraft that launch for perimeter mapping once the incident escalates. I'm also thinking through whether adding drone units creates new draw calls or just more markers within the existing rendering budget, and whether TALON should auto-send an intel package (GPS, thermal map, wind, approach route) to responding fire units as a pre-approved, low-risk action logged in the feed. For surfacing autonomy, I'm leaning toward a "Quiet/Normal/Critical" attention indicator plus a collapsed feed ("3 autonomous actions — show") and an explicit strip listing what TALON and drones are doing right now, so operators always know what's happening without being overwhelmed. Each entry in that strip would get per-row controls — details, talk, take control, stop — borrowing the pattern from One's thread list rows so intervention is always one click away. I'm also mapping trust concerns to UI elements: confidence and provenance for "trust the autonomous response," visible uncertainty indicators for "false confidence," and the authority model plus intervene/undo controls for "loss of control." On branding, I'm wondering whether to fold in FlytBase identity alongside Sentinel/TALON, though the user's current ask seems focused on the TALON mascot/logo rather than full FlytBase branding. I'll skip FlytBase's actual branding and just note it in the summary as a separate deliverable the user can add. For the design direction, I'm leaning into dark, calm, precise glass aesthetics with One's dot language and a minimal mascot, keeping playfulness confined to micro-motion rather than overt styling. A Three.js (r170) terrain and map engine for emergency command displays, plus a player that runs an incident as a timeline. Three tiers:

| tier | file | knows about |

| 1 · engine | `terrainEngine.ts` | terrain, vegetation, roads, structures, generic layers (line, polygon, points, marker, labels, time-of-arrival field), units, cameras, drone feed. Nothing about fires, plans or incidents. |

ThinkingOn a modern GPU, applying blur and saturation to three elements — topbar, TALON panel, dock widgets — should be fine, though it'll be sluggish under headless SwiftShader testing, which doesn't matter for real use. Now I want to check applyCamera and the camera objects.
I'm thinking about how the PiP element works as a DOM overlay with a scissor-rendered canvas view, and considering whether placing the feed in the bottom dock widget still works if the canvas renders full-bleed behind it, since the scissor rect could just be positioned wherever the dock sits. For the dock implementation, I'd need an engine API like `setPipHost(el)` that places the PiP element inside the dock widget instead of floating freely, computing its rect from the host's bounding box relative to the canvas. The tricky part is the dock's glass backdrop blur—the feed area itself needs to stay transparent so the canvas shows through unblurred while the rest of the panel keeps its glass effect. The fix is to keep the dock container itself transparent and give each widget card its own backdrop-filter individually, except the feed card, which stays unblurred with just a frame border. I also need to make sure `updateDom` hides the map DOM elements under the PiP box, and that `hasAnimatedContent` keeps rendering at 30fps while the feed is open. I'm now weighing dock sizing: a 16:9 feed widget at reasonable width eats a lot of vertical space, so I'm sketching out row heights for the timeline and widget area to see if the dock stays under roughly 270px total, versus letting the feed float as a PiP over the map instead. For the floating approach, I'm designing an engine API that lets a drone PiP be hosted inside an arbitrary container element—filling it statically rather than dragging freely—while still reusing the engine's rect calculations, though I need to handle cases where that host sits outside the normal canvas bounds. I'm also thinking through container setup: since the engine attaches canvas, overlays, and a ResizeObserver to its container, floating UI panels just need higher z-index to sit above those overlays. For proper camera framing around panels, I want to add a view-inset method that shifts the camera's principal point to recenter the visible scene. To do this I'm considering using the camera's setViewOffset technique — treating the actual render as a sub-window of a larger virtual frame, so the padded region is excluded and the effective visual center shifts away from the raw canvas center. So the call becomes setViewOffset(W, H, (right-left)/2, (bottom-top)/2, W, H), and since raycasting and DOM projection both rely on the camera's projection matrix, they'll stay consistent automatically. I do need to watch for other engine code that might assume a symmetric frustum, like ground-extent calculations for LOD or label culling logic. I also need to handle the topdown ortho-like camera similarly, and figure out where applyCamera sets aspect/updateProjectionMatrix so I know where to apply or clear the view offset. Actually, maybe the simplest fix is avoiding full-bleed entirely — if the map container is just the grid region between panels, no view offset is needed at all. But that trades away the premium floating-glass-over-full-bleed-map look that defines modern command UIs. I think full-bleed with insets is worth it, so I'll add generic, incident-agnostic engine features: setViewInsets and a PiP host option. For the glass panel over the map, I'm weighing the cost of backdrop-filter blur recompositing every frame at 30fps against the visual payoff. On a modern GPU, applying blur and saturation to three elements — topbar, TALON panel, dock widgets — should be fine, though it'll be sluggish under headless SwiftShader testing, which doesn't matter for real use. Now I want to check applyCamera and the camera objects.

I'm figuring out that camera height in metres applies to both ortho and perspective modes, and that view offsets can be used in both—ortho cameras support asymmetric left/right/top/bottom shifts, while perspective cameras use setViewOffset with width, height, and offset coordinates, keeping the vertical field of view consistent across the full view. Now I'm thinking through how "in effect" decisions resolve relative to time t, how committedAt(t) derives from the authorize decision via generic ref resolution, and the tricky question of what happens when authorize() fires before a phase's nominal time—whether to jump the clock forward to that phase or just show authorization status separately while the phase label stays put. I'm leaning toward avoiding a jarring time skip and instead keeping the clock where it is while marking the decision as committed. That means reworking PhaseDef so phases have both a nominal time and an optional dependency on a decision reference, so a phase can't begin until that decision has occurred even if its nominal time hasn't arrived yet. With monotonic start times enforced across phases, if authorization comes early, E simply starts at its nominal time with no jump; if it comes late, E starts at the authorization time and any subsequent phase with an equal or earlier nominal time collapses into it, effectively skipping E, which seems like an acceptable edge case. If authorization never happens, E (and anything after it) just never starts, leaving the sequence stuck at D. This feels semantically correct: without authorization, no further operations should fire even though time-based elements like fire growth or TALON's scheduled events continue unless explicitly gated. The remaining question is about the route cut scenario — since the plan draft logic can set a draft route even before commitment, I need to check whether an uncommitted draft would still render visually despite authorization never completing. I think I'll handle this by gating the draft decision on authorization directly, and let phases/decisions carry an optional `when` or `after` reference that must resolve before they apply. I'll also add an optional `shift` property for units so tracks and patches can be offset relative to a reference time like authorization. I realize item ids containing hyphens could collide with the offset parsing, since something like "item-2" might get misread as an offset of -2, so I'm deciding to avoid hyphens and trailing digits in ids, sticking to plain alphabetic names like 'escalate', 'plan', 'draft', 'prepos', 'detect', 'stall', and 'release' to keep the parsing unambiguous. I'm also thinking the time reference syntax should generalize to "base ± offset" where the base can be either a phase id or a decision reference, parsed with a regex that splits off a trailing signed number. Then I'm sketching out the Decision type as a tagged union covering kinds like primary, draft, approve, reject, authorize, and answer, each carrying relevant fields like route, actor, note, and timing. Now I'm working through actor semantics: operator-only decisions like approve should only apply when autopilot is enabled, with draft defaulting to talon and everything else defaulting to operator, and I'm adjusting the harness to set autopilot true so existing playback behavior still holds. I also want decisions to support a `when` guard so, for example, a draft only applies if the plan was previously authorized, which means resolving these references in time order using only decisions already accepted at or before that point. For resolving refs like '@authorize' or '@approve', I'm treating them as the earliest accepted matching decision at or before the given time, with item answers using first-wins semantics unless an earlier re-answer truncates and replaces later overrides. Since this effective-decisions computation gets called often during resolution, I want to cache it per timestamp by building a shared context object once per resolve call rather than recomputing repeatedly. I'm now working through how phase starts should be computed monotonically, where each phase's start is the max of the previous phase's start, its nominal time, and any 'after' reference it depends on, while being careful that phase-id refs only resolve to decision-aware starts to avoid circular dependencies with other phase 'after' refs. Checking the scenario where authorization never happens pushes phase starts to infinity, meaning the plan is never committed and the system correctly escalates after the gate expires. I'm also adding a guard to the authorize() API so it only takes effect when called during a phase with an active gate, rather than jumping time or committing prematurely if called too early. I'm deciding against auto-advancing to phase E upon authorization in the console, since live time naturally progresses there anyway, while still allowing an optional jump behavior for the harness's presenter flow. I'm also computing gate-open status based on the most recent phase with a defined gate, so the UI reflects the correct state even if the operator is viewing a later phase before authorization occurs. Now I'm sketching out the answer-recording API: `answer()` locks in the first decision unless rewound, `answerOf()` retrieves it, and `getDecisions()` aggregates accepted choices tagged by source (script vs operator) for the ledger. I'm also designing a time-shift mechanism for units and layers, where a computed offset gets applied to patches, states, and tracks, while `from`/`until` bounds stay anchored to raw time references, plus a boards system where `boardAt()` looks up the latest keyframe at or before a given time. Board, zone-label, and unit patches can rely on offset-based refs directly without needing the shift logic, since only continuous tracks require the computed offset. I'm adding a `hindsight` mode that swaps in alternate `from`/`until` bounds on layers for retrospective views, plus `setTime()` with fade support, expanded `PlayerState` fields for units and autopilot, and a `phaseStart()` method so the console can query decision-aware phase timing while change events fire on autopilot/hindsight toggles. Now I'm defining the TalonState interface with agents, an open-items queue for things needing operator attention, chronological feed/log entries, mood, and suggested dock widgets, along with supporting types for open items and log entries. The return shape includes a reply string plus optional evidence, focus, and action fields. resume and try to finish the whole build end to end with pixel perfection. a few things i reviewed so far between the build session and before completetion- Where it drifts — four gaps, ranked 1. No dissent record, no re-raise. This is the big one. The constitution's core is that a refusal is preserved — TALON's position and the operator's, verbatim — and that a later re-raise cites only the new evidence and routes to a second authority (the Regional Duty Supervisor). The model has a log with who: 'talon' | 'operator' and kind: 'reply', so there's a transcript, but no preserved dissent record and no re-raise at all. The refusal path is the product (doc 13 §2) and it is the part most likely to get quietly dropped, because a transcript looks like a record. 2. No interrupt rate budget. One-at-a-time is not ≤2 per 10 minutes. Our repo's ISA-18.2 budget is the most-tested law we have (19 contract checks in verify:attention), and the new arbiter reimplements attention outside the repo without the rate cap. Twenty well-spaced interrupts would pass this model. 3. kind: 'auto' and authority: 'auto' — a path where TALON acts unprompted. TalonEffect includes route, and at L355 it applies unconditionally. Meanwhile the draft/approve/reject path also exists. So both a self-applying route change and an operator-approved one are live. That's fine for scenario scripting but it contradicts doc 13's "it never executes" unless auto is scoped hard: auto may only mean "within a pre-authorized run card" — never "unprompted." The naming currently reads as the latter. 4. authority: 'operator+legal' is an unruled governance tier. It doesn't exist in the repo's model and has no owner ruling. Either it goes in DECISIONS.md or it goes. The structural warning There are now two attention models. The repo has domain/attention.ts (19 contract checks), domain/talonSurface.ts, and eval:talon (42 cases). The new project has its own arbiter in talon.ts. This is the exact pattern we've been killing all along — three renderers, two coordinate laws, two fire geometries. The new arbiter must eventually replace the old one, not sit beside it. That's a decision to write down now, before it calcifies. Same for Review / ReviewRow / CommandFacts / CommandResult in talon.ts, which overlap the repo's Ics209DebriefModal and DebriefTimeline. Improvement notes Beyond the constitution, the model got genuinely better in ways worth keeping: Provenance is now a type, not a convention. basis on telemetry means a surface cannot render a measurement without saying where it came from. That's §1.3 enforced by the compiler. Multiple named agents with roles opens a door our single-TALON model didn't have — and it maps onto the mutual-aid phase, where authority and ground teams genuinely differ. Mood including 'sheepish' — for an AI that has just been overridden, that's a small, humane detail. Worth keeping, with the caveat that it must not read as apologetic about everything. hold — playback pausing at an unanswered item is a good harness mechanic. But it and autopilot are the phase player in new clothes: autopilot is literally "the script plays itself." Both must be harness-only. They sit right against the ruling that the flow must not be a visible surface. so lets move forward now make this system an overall masterpiece of design and product thinking with proper UI/UX laws applied as well and a consistent design system i dont want random hex and values.

ThinkingTo fix implicit any errors under strict mode I'll annotate the parameters, and I'm quickly checking the engine's exports for loadWorldData and generateProceduralWorld to confirm they're available.
I'm setting up index.html with the import map, fonts, CSS links, and SVG mascot definitions, then moving into writing the main command console module that imports the terrain engine and scenario player. Now I'm planning out the console's structure: helper functions, inline icon SVGs, the mascot graphic, and a UI state object tracking things like the active tab, pinned items, playback speed, and selection state. I'm also sketching the boot sequence that loads world data and mounts a scenario by creating the terrain engine and scenario player together. After that I'm mapping the render loop — computing player and talon state, then rendering each UI section (topbar, rail, panel, dock, inspector) along with attention overlays on the map. I still need to work through event delegation, resize handling, the growth chart, sound and voice features, onboarding, and a piecewise timeline scale built from phase timings. For the timeline, I'm weighting each segment by the square root of its duration so dense phases get proportionally more space without hard-coded ratios, then only showing T-labels at anchor points with enough spacing to avoid overlap. Playback advances position based on speed over a 90-second total duration, pausing at holds unless autopilot is active. For the feed drone selection, I'm falling back through operator choice, suggestion, then first airborne drone, defaulting sensor to 'eo', and opening or closing the picture-in-picture feed based on widget visibility—making sure to pick an airborne drone rather than a docked one. For the dock layout, I'm computing column count from available width (4 columns above 1180px, down to 1 column for narrow widths). Now I'm working out how many op-slots versus talon-slots each column count gets, then figuring pinned widgets (defaulting to weather and fleet), filtering TALON suggestions by availability and pinning status, and falling back to a priority order of feed, evac, growth, events, fleet, weather when slots need filling. I'm defining availability rules for each widget type—feed needs an airborne drone, evac needs a non-null board, growth needs a fire layer present, while events, fleet, and weather are always available. For the actual widget rendering, I'm laying out the weather widget's cells (wind direction arrow, humidity, temp, fuel, status, spread, provenance chip) and starting on the fleet widget's row structure with unit icons by kind, ID, and details. Now I'm continuing the fleet row rendering with status dots and eta/battery, then moving through evac's zone bars and route rows with choke points and alerts, growth's SVG chart, and the events widget which pulls milestones from timeline markers—clicking a past milestone in review mode jumps time, while in live mode it scrubs backward into past-viewing. I'm working out the live-versus-viewing-past distinction: ui.liveT tracks the furthest time reached by playback, and when the current time falls meaningfully behind that, the UI should show a "Viewing T+..." state with a "Back to live" button. To keep decision-making safe, I'm disabling option buttons while viewing the past, with a hint telling users to return to live first. I'm also sketching review mode — a dedicated panel tab, a LIVE→REVIEW topbar swap, disabled decisions, a hindsight toggle, and free timeline scrubbing that snaps back to liveT on exit. Then I start on the inspector panel, which opens from clicking a layer, unit, or falling back to a map click. For the inspector's layer view, I'm pulling the player state entry (group, state, provenance, timestamps) plus the situation layer definition and owner mapping, then deciding which action buttons to show — "Make primary" for unauthorized routes when the gate is open, or "Propose as primary" for committed ones. For units I'm adding a message action with a prefilled mention, a feed link for drones, and a fly-to option. For zones I'm checking point-in-polygon against situation layer rings to detect evac-order, warning, or safe states, and for a bare location I'm pulling elevation, slope, cover, fuel, and fire state from an engine pick. I'm also designing the attention marker system: when there's an active attention target or hovered evidence, I place a violet-toned focus marker at the relevant position with a "TALON · label" title, and I emphasize the related layers plus the focus marker and labels while hovering, clearing that emphasis on mouse-leave. Persistent (non-hover) attention just leaves the marker without emphasis, and the mascot's gaze shifts to the map during evidence hovering. Now I'm wiring up fleet row hovering to highlight the corresponding unit on the engine, and setting up camera-follow behavior so the view flies to a phase's camera on phase changes or to an evidence point when "Show on map" is clicked. I'm also working out how to compute UI insets from the DOM — accounting for the topbar, the TALON panel width, and the dock height, including a mobile case where TALON becomes a bottom sheet — and exposing the TALON width and dock height as CSS custom properties so the layout can react to them. Finally, I'm mapping out keyboard shortcuts: number keys for selecting answer options, space for play/pause, slash to focus the composer, and escape to close open popovers or inspectors. Beyond those shortcuts, I'm defining more key bindings for lighting, IR map, 2D/3D toggle, review mode, TALON panel toggle, and stepping through exercise beats. I'm also designing the dissent flow — when someone picks a non-recommended option, a box appears explaining both positions go on record, with an optional reasoning textarea and cancel/record buttons, plus keyboard equivalents for opening and submitting it. Then I'm working through interrupt notifications: new items trigger a chime and toast with a pulsing rail indicator, tracked via a set of seen ids that resets on situation changes or backward scrubbing, and I'm sketching the re-raise card that shows escalation status, new evidence, and the original dissent record. Now I'm fleshing out the Review tab (measures grid, decisions list, dissent records, hindsight toggle, replay option) and the Log tab with its agent filter chips. For the mascot, I'm designing an SVG shield-like face with slanted slit eyes giving it a refined, raptor-like look, using gradient fills for the rim and face. Now I'm working out the eye rotation details — tilting the inner end of each slit eye down slightly to suggest a focused, stern expression versus tilting it up for a friendlier, more concerned look, settling on a subtle clockwise rotation for the stern variant. I realize the CSS transform for blinking would override any SVG rotation attribute, so I need to wrap each eye in a group element to handle the rotation separately from the blink animation. Then I'm sketching a brand mark concept — a ring with a chevron-like aperture shape and a small dot below it — before moving on to designing a set of simple stroke-based icons like play, pause, skip controls, inbox, and chat. Now I'm planning out a large icon set covering things like mic, shield, gear, layers, sun/moon, flame, cube/square toggles, plus/minus, compass, target, close, chevrons, pin, eye, send, drone, truck, crew, dozer, badge, and various utility glyphs. With that settled, I'm moving on to writing commandConsole.ts, which is going to be a large file, so I'm keeping TypeScript loose with `any` where needed to avoid strictness issues like unused locals. The Sentinel console with TALON is built end to end and passes all 20 headless checks. Run npm run serve and open http://127.0.0.1:8130/. Everything left open is in HANDOFF.md in tactical-terrain/.

What you get

  • Layout: global status runs along the top and the 3D map sits in the middle, centred in the space the panels leave. TALON is on the right with agent status dots, an inbox, a thread and a composer. The bottom dock has an incident timeline plus widget slots: drone feed, weather, fleet, evacuation, fire growth, key events. Your pinned slots stay put; TALON only fills its own labelled slots.
  • TALON's decision cards: each card carries its evidence and highlights it on the map when you hover. The plan card shows two courses of action side by side, the gated order with how many people it reaches and the geofence check, and a countdown. You answer with keys 1–3.
  • The arc: detection at 03:47 → plan proposed at 6:00 → order issued about 1–2 minutes later, depending on when you decide (7:48 on the autopilot run). The review shows that against the brief's 38-minute manual baseline. Later in the run TALON says "I was wrong": a drone finds a spot fire and the road cut comes 14 minutes earlier than projected.
  • Review mode: the timing measures, every decision, the dissent records and a hindsight overlay. The map and the panel show exactly what you saw at each moment.
  • Design system: every colour, space, radius, type size and timing value is a token defined once in console.css. The chart colours pass the colour-blindness validator.
  • Screens: built for 1280 px and wider; the phone layout is removed as you asked.

Your four review points, all in place and tested

  1. Dissent and re-raise: declining TALON's recommendation records both positions verbatim, including your own words. A later re-raise cites only new evidence and goes to the Regional Duty Supervisor; the operator can't answer it.
  2. Interrupt budget: at most 2 interrupts per 10 minutes. Extra ones are downgraded and the downgrade is logged. Across the whole run the worst 10-minute window has 1.
  3. Authority: only two tiers, "standing order" and "operator". A standing-order action that doesn't cite its order is dropped. Effects run only when you pick an option; a TALON draft never executes.
  4. operator+legal is removed.

Autopilot and the clock that pauses for your decision sit only in a dashed "EXERCISE" group, and the incident phases never appear as steps in the product.

  • Decisions for you:
    • the attention model in talon.ts should replace domain/attention.ts, not sit beside it;
    • which debrief model is canonical;
    • whether "Regional Duty Supervisor" is the right name for the second authority;
    • whether keeping phase ids inside the data satisfies "the flow must not be a visible surface".
  • Only partly looked at: I checked seven states across 1280, 1440 and 1920 widths. Day lighting, 2D mode, the Log tab, the popovers, onboarding, 4K and ultra-wide weren't checked.

  • Prototype limits: TALON's replies are scripted, not a model. The fire spread is a simple growth model, not a real fire-behaviour model.
  • Docs and tooling: npm run phases and README.md still describe the old harness flow; HANDOFF.md is the current source.
